cards.hook: Toughness = **how unlikely a bad event is to change your behaviour against your goals**. Four separate dials.

items: how much before you snap (your fuse)
how big the change when you snap
how fast you're back to baseline
is the new baseline higher or lower?
vis.note: Rate yourself low/medium/high on each. Train the weakest one.

cards.plain: You can be great at one and weak at another. He wrote this for himself after his mother died weeks after his biggest launch. Rule: change as little as possible, keep the things that make you feel better.
cards.analogy: Losing a set: tolerance = how many bad points before you tilt; fortitude = do you just sigh or smash the racket; resilience = back to normal next game or next week; adaptability = do you play better after.
cards.ex: "My emotional discomfort is not an adequate reason to change what I'm doing."
cards.move: A dead dial block lowers your mood, not your plan. Same blocks tomorrow. Pick your weakest dial and train it on purpose.
cards.trap: Thinking toughness = not feeling. It's not changing behaviour because of the feeling.
q: Which dial is "how fast you're back"?
Resilience.
What's trauma by his definition?
A lasting change in behaviour caused by a bad event; it can go either way.
clip: The four parts of mental toughness

cards.hook: Influence = how likely people do what you ask. Stack **Status, Power, Credibility, Likeness**.

items: you control something scarce they want
you said do X, it worked, they trust the next ask
proof a third party can see

cards.plain: Each letter is a dial and mostly works in one domain. Power is the one he'd keep: every time your advice works for someone, your next request is easier.
cards.analogy: Your parents max all four, which is why their requests still pull on you.
cards.ex: A trust-fund kid has status; a kid who gave you 10 stock picks that all worked has status + power: far more influence.
cards.move: Every owner call: give one specific hiring tip they can use this week. When it works, the Bench Trial ask is easier.
cards.trap: Chasing views (no status, no power) instead of results for the right people.
q: Which letter matters most to him?
Power: say-do-it-worked cycles.

cards.hook: Courage = **taking action with a big short-term cost for an uncertain, delayed benefit**. Your potential = uncertainty tolerated × how long.
cards.plain: Smart people stay stuck because they won't act without certainty. The path you're on is guaranteed not to get you there; the other isn't guaranteed but is the only one with a shot.
cards.analogy: Going for the line on break point. Playing safe guarantees you don't win the point.
cards.ex: Beat 99% by mastering three things: the shame of rejection, the boredom of repetition, the pain of feedback.
cards.move: Every dial is a courage rep. Count them as such.
cards.trap: Waiting to feel ready.
q: The 3 things to master to beat 99%?
Shame of rejection, boredom of repetition, pain of feedback.

cards.hook: "Decide" comes from **"to cut off"**. Options only have value when you exercise one.
cards.plain: Commitment is the elimination of alternatives. Keeping every option open is itself a choice: the choice of getting nothing.
cards.analogy: You can't train for tennis, football and swimming at full level. Pick one and the others become hobbies.
cards.ex: Leila: you can't have a lifelong partner and maximum optionality.
cards.move: No new business ideas until 100 owner conversations. That rule IS the cut-off. Write it in your decision document.
cards.trap: Re-deciding every week.
q: What's the hidden cost of not deciding?
You keep paying in attention while nothing compounds; doors close anyway.
clip: Options only have value when taken

cards.hook: Fear is **a mile wide and an inch deep**. Write the failure out step by step and it shrinks.

vis.title: Make it specific
steps: what exactly happens, day by day

cards.plain: Your brain overprices vague risks. When you write the concrete worst case, it's almost always survivable. In the developed world, the downside of trying hard is close to zero.
cards.analogy: Playing a "scary" opponent: watch one of their matches and they become a person with a weak backhand.
cards.ex: He asked a friend in advance: "if this blows up, can I crash on your couch?" A yes let him jump.
cards.move: Write what actually happens if an owner says no on the phone. Answer: nothing. Then dial.
cards.trap: Keeping fear in your head where it stays big.
q: How do you shrink a fear?
Write the worst case step by step and a plan B.

cards.hook: **Pivot only when a founding assumption is proven false** by real feedback. Otherwise it's execution: push.

steps: is a core assumption proven false?
change the assumption, keep the skills

cards.plain: Most plans die from too little volume for too little time, not from a wrong idea. Decide leading indicators up front so you can keep pushing before results.
cards.analogy: Missing first serves? Practise more before deciding you're "not a serve-and-volley player".
cards.ex: 100 dog owners and none want the dog skateboard = assumption false → pivot.
cards.move: If 100 owners say they have no hiring problem, pivot. If they have it and don't buy yet: push (offer, script, volume).
cards.trap: Pivoting at the first boredom or bad week.
q: When is a pivot justified?
When real feedback disproves a founding assumption.

cards.hook: ~**3 days a month are bottom-10% days for no reason**. Don't quit on a red square.

vis.title: A normal month
vis.note: Bad days are guaranteed by maths. A bad day where you still did the work is a good day.

cards.plain: Moods are weather. Judge yourself by actions despite feelings. Only suffer once: life shoots the first arrow, don't shoot the second by reliving it.
cards.analogy: Even the best players have days the ball won't land. They play the next match.
cards.ex: Ackman in a terrible year: make some progress every day; at 30 and 90 days it shows.
cards.move: On a bottom-10% day: the minimum (10 dials + 25 min BAC) and sleep. Nothing gets decided that day.
cards.trap: Making big decisions on a red day.
q: What's the second arrow?
Suffering again by reliving and judging the first pain.

cards.hook: No silver bullet: **hundreds of tiny details done right**. And today's "a lot" should become tomorrow's minimum.

vis.title: His standard over time
vis.note: The minimum rose ~100×. Measure work in hundreds of reps.

cards.plain: Great products are 100 small things nobody else bothers with. Real perfectionists finish; fake ones procrastinate. Pick where to be uncompromising (highest leverage) and use volume everywhere else.
cards.analogy: A pro's serve is 100 details: toss height, knee bend, grip, pronation…
cards.ex: "But I'll know" beats "what will they think?"
cards.move: Your minimum: 150 dials/week. In a month, make that the floor and the next step the stretch.
cards.trap: Perfecting the website instead of perfecting the call.
q: Where should you refuse to compromise?
Where leverage is highest; use volume elsewhere.

cards.hook: Focus isn't willpower. **Remove everything else** so the work is the most interesting thing left.
cards.plain: In a white room with one black dot, the dot gets all your attention. Arrange your environment so work is the dot. Use a kitchen timer and stop it whenever you check your phone.
cards.analogy: Practising serves alone on court vs with your phone buzzing on the bench.
cards.ex: People delay starting longer than the task takes. Starting is the perfect condition.
cards.move: Dial blocks: only dialer and script open; phone with apps in another room.
cards.trap: Productivity apps (adding) to fix focus.
q: What does the kitchen timer measure?
Real time on task: it stops when you check your phone.

cards.hook: **"If you're nervous, do more."** Do it until you're bored; then you're ready.
cards.plain: Nerves come from uncertainty. Reps remove uncertainty. He rehearsed the launch 100+ times and was the calmest person backstage.
cards.analogy: First match nerves vanish by the 50th match.
cards.ex: Volume negates luck: one of the two credos in Acquisition.com's sales handbook.
cards.move: Read the opener out loud before each block; the dials themselves are the reps.
cards.trap: Waiting until you feel confident to start.
q: Cure for nerves?
More reps until it's boring.

cards.hook: Time is zero-sum. **You pick your regrets or they get picked for you.**
cards.plain: Every hour on one area comes from another. You'll live an imperfect life either way, so choose which imperfections on purpose.
cards.analogy: You can't be at a tournament and your friend's birthday. Choose, don't drift.
cards.ex: He lifts with friends he works with: three boxes with one activity.
cards.move: Your ranking is clear: agency → BAC → sleep/health → tennis coaching. When a day breaks, cut in that reverse order.
cards.trap: Saying yes to everything and regretting everything a little.
q: How do you tick several boxes at once?
Combine areas in one activity (train with friends, coach to earn).

cards.hook: Respect = **letting someone's words change what you do when they can't make you**. Earn it with POWERS, give it with HEARTED.

items: known rule + could + chose not → consequence

cards.plain: Enforcement alone = tyrant. Competence without enforcement = admired doormat. Give respect with HEARTED: Honor, Esteem, Attend, Reliable, Truth, Expectations, Defer.
cards.analogy: The coach kids respect: works hardest, keeps promises, is fair with rules, calm in tough moments.
cards.ex: He volunteered to go with a pledge to the feared hazer: paying the cost where everyone saw it.
cards.move: With caregivers and owners: Word is everything. Every promise (callback, replacement in 24h) kept, every time.
cards.trap: Trying to be liked instead of respected.
q: What 3 things must be true to enforce fairly?
The standard was known, could be met, and they chose not to.

cards.hook: The fastest way to $10M **isn't** the fastest way to $100M. **The height decides the foundation.**

vis.title: Time you have → base you build

cards.plain: If you only have 30 seconds you stack blocks fast and it falls. With 5 years you dig foundations first: customers who stay, a product people refer. Focus and patience are anti-human, so they're lasting edges.
cards.analogy: Juniors who only learn to win now (moonballs) plateau; those who build proper technique peak later and higher.
cards.ex: Company A keeps its 100 customers a year; B churns them and must sell 600 next year to stand still.
cards.move: Build Caregiver Bench to keep agencies for years: retention beats a quick sales spike.
cards.trap: Tactics that win this month and cap you forever.
q: What's the anti-human edge?
Focus and patience.
clip: The blocks exercise: build for 50 years

cards.t: "What will this change about my day?"
cards.hook: Before a scary decision ask: **will it make me start things I don't want, or stop things I do?** Usually no, so the stakes are imaginary.

steps: what changes in my actual day?

cards.plain: Most decisions feel huge but don't change your daily life. Save your energy for the few that do.
cards.analogy: Changing string brand vs changing coach: only one changes your weekly practice.
cards.ex: His most practical risk filter (Mylett 2026).
cards.move: New idea or purchase: does it add or remove dials/BAC hours? If not, decide in a minute. If it lowers the goal's odds: no.
cards.trap: Agonising over decisions that don't touch your day.
cards.memo: **"No change to my day = no drama."**
q: When do you spend time on a decision?
Only when it changes what you do day to day.
clip: What will this change about my day?

cards.hook: You've only learned when **the same situation now gets a different response from you**.
cards.plain: Knowing isn't learning. Intelligence = speed of learning, so you can compensate by doing more iterations. Flat results for 6+ months while working hard = you haven't learned.
cards.analogy: You "know" to bend your knees; you've learned when your knees bend on a low ball in a match.
cards.ex: After ~10 self-help books he lived in the same condo with the same job: zero learning.
cards.move: After each dial block, write one thing you'll do differently next block. Then do it.
cards.trap: Collecting knowledge (like these cards) without changing a behaviour.
q: Sign you haven't learned?
Same conditions, same behaviour, same results.

cards.hook: In hard times, picture telling the story at 80: **the bigger the dragon, the better the story.**
cards.plain: Stories raise the value of the hard behaviour right now, like an ad raises the value of a product. The main listener of your stories is you.
cards.analogy: The matches you remember are the comebacks from 1–5 down.
cards.ex: Great stories start with conflict.
cards.move: Document the hard parts (screenshots, voice notes): that's your journey content later.
cards.trap: Treating the hard chapter as proof you're failing.
q: Who's the main listener of your stories?
You.

cards.hook: Delaying gratification is a skill, but **delaying forever means you never collect**. Optimise across your life.
cards.plain: Top performers can delay forever. Know when to cash some chips: hold the tension between consuming now and investing for later.
cards.analogy: Training so hard you never play a tournament.
cards.ex: Glasses he saved 8 weeks for and never wore; a summer in Paris without a single croissant.
cards.move: Plan small, deliberate rewards (a good meal after a 70-dial Thursday) so the machine keeps running.
cards.trap: Thinking every pleasure is weakness.
q: What's the third marshmallow fallacy?
Delaying forever and never collecting.

cards.t: No one is coming to save you
cards.hook: Three steps to win: **no one is coming; take responsibility for your position; sacrifice who you are for who you want to be.**

steps: not your fault, still your problem

cards.plain: Blame gives your power to people you don't control. Responsibility gives it back. At 19 he realised blaming his parents gave people he resented power over his success.
cards.analogy: The umpire made a bad call. You still have to win the next point.
cards.ex: Poverty's first lesson: "my fault" (Modern Wisdom 2023).
cards.move: When a week goes badly, write: what did I control, and what will I do differently Monday?
cards.trap: Confusing responsibility with blame and beating yourself up.
q: Difference between fault and responsibility?
Fault is about the past; responsibility is about what you do next.

cards.t: Hopeless vs anxious vs a quest
cards.hook: Hopeless = **no options**: build capacity. Anxious = **too many**: pick one. A quest = one clear path.
cards.plain: When you don't know what to do, dig the well before you're thirsty (skills, savings, health). When you know too many things to do, choose one and cut the rest.
cards.analogy: A player with no tournaments trains; a player entered in 6 at once picks the one that matters.
cards.ex: He got through hopeless periods by doing the task in front of him and building capacity.
cards.move: You're on a quest: Caregiver Bench to $20k MRR. When anxious, re-read the decision doc and cut.
cards.trap: Treating anxiety (too many options) with more options.
q: Cure for hopelessness?
Build capacity: sleep, train, save, prepare.

cards.t: Model the climb, not the summit
m: what (they|did they) do at your stage
cards.hook: Don't copy a winner's **current** life. Ask **what they did at your stage**.

b: "stuff I hated, nobody rooting for me"

cards.plain: Successful people's routines today are rewards for years of different behaviour. Copying the summit routine at the bottom keeps you at the bottom.
cards.analogy: Pros train 2h a day now; at 14 they played 5h a day.
cards.ex: Raise Your Standards (Modern Wisdom): ask successful people what they did at your stage.
cards.move: Your stage = high volume, low leverage: dials, scripts, learning. Fancy systems come later.
cards.trap: Optimising mornings like a billionaire before your first customer.
q: What question do you ask a successful person?
What did you do at my stage?

cards.hook: Make sure you're **winning your own game**, not someone else's scoreboard.

b: "would I do this if nobody saw?"

cards.plain: He spent years trying to out-earn his father. When his dad apologised, he felt nothing: he'd been winning his dad's game. Define your own rules.
cards.analogy: Playing for the ranking points your coach wants vs the style you love.
cards.ex: Don't change direction just to beat someone at the game they care about.
cards.move: Your goals (2027 roadmap) are yours. Check them against "who am I trying to impress?" once a month.
cards.trap: Using spite as the only fuel; it runs out after you "win".
q: Sign you're in someone else's game?
Winning feels empty; the goal was to prove something to them.

cards.hook: Work capacity grows like muscle: **load it, recover, load more**. Burnout is mostly rushing, not volume.
cards.plain: "Once you look like you work out, you can worry about overtraining." Real burnout = output per hour dropping. Most "burnout" is an arbitrary deadline.
cards.analogy: Fitness base: you don't start with 3-hour sessions, but you build to them.
cards.ex: Burnout = rushing (1/0 live); work capacity is trainable (Be Ruthless).
cards.move: Increase dials gradually (150 → 225 when the Florida slot exists). Protect sleep 21:00–06:00: that's recovery.
cards.trap: Calling a hard week "burnout" and stopping.
q: Real sign of burnout?
Output per unit of time dropping, measurably.

cards.t: Listen to people closest to your goal
m: if they don.t have what you want
cards.hook: Take advice from people **closest to your goals**, not closest to you.
cards.plain: People who love you want you safe; their advice minimises risk, not maximises outcome. If they don't have what you want, don't take their directions.
cards.analogy: Technique advice from a club pro, not from your uncle who watches Wimbledon.
cards.ex: If they don't have what you want, don't listen (Be Ruthless).
cards.move: Agency owners' feedback on calls > friends' opinions about cold calling.
cards.trap: Ignoring everyone (including good critics). Filter by evidence, not by feelings.
q: Who gets a vote on your plan?
People who have achieved what you want.
clip: If they don't have what you want, don't listen

cards.hook: Growing means a phase where you're **too big for the old group and not yet in the new one**. Everyone passes through it.
cards.plain: It repeats on every mountain, often right after a first success. Find communities of people ahead of you and give first.
cards.analogy: Moving up a ranking category: the old practice partners are too easy, the new ones don't know you yet.
cards.ex: The lonely middle (I'm 37 stream).
cards.move: Join one community of agency founders/cold callers; contribute one useful post a week.
cards.trap: Shrinking back to fit the old group.
q: What's the exit?
A new group whose minimum standards are your goals.

cards.hook: When everything feels heavy, **win the next small thing**. String good days together.
cards.plain: Big goals freeze you; small wins build momentum. In some seasons maintaining is winning.
cards.analogy: Down 1–5: play one point at a time.
cards.ex: Mental toughness hotline: one W at a time. Ackman: progress every day; it shows at 30 and 90 days.
cards.move: Minimum day: 10 dials + 25 min BAC. It's still a W.
cards.trap: All-or-nothing days.
q: What counts on a bad day?
The minimum, done.

cards.hook: The easiest fix when life sucks: **change the environment**, and behaviour follows.
cards.plain: Behaviour is shaped by cues and rewards around you. Even small changes (another room, another city, phone elsewhere) shift loops.
cards.analogy: Practising at a court with a ball machine vs a park court full of distractions.
cards.ex: Even two miles down the road or moving out of your mom's basement counts (Modern Wisdom 2023).
cards.move: Dial blocks: same desk, same time, phone out. Your relocation plan (July 2027) is the big version.
cards.trap: Relying on willpower in a bad environment.
q: Why environment over willpower?
Cues and rewards drive behaviour automatically.

cards.hook: Same backstory, two endings: **the villain is used by pain, the hero uses it.**

a: "the world hurt me, so I'll hurt it"
b: "the world hurt me, so I'll fix it"

cards.plain: Pain is fuel if pointed at a goal. Negative visualisation (10 more years of this?) can make current pain big enough to act.
cards.analogy: A painful loss that makes you train harder vs one that makes you quit.
cards.ex: Heroes use pain, villains are used by it (Be Ruthless); pain as fuel (Success Is a Side Effect).
cards.move: When you feel behind, picture July 2027 with no agency revenue. Let it push the next block.
cards.trap: Letting pain become identity.
q: What's negative visualisation?
Imagining the future if nothing changes, to make the pain actionable.

cards.hook: A business grows like a body: **each headcount stage has one problem to solve**, and the founder has to change roles to graduate.

vis.title: Stage = headcount = your role
rungs: 0 people · researcher · get people to try it free
vis.note: You are on rung 1 (glowing): the only job is the first paying agency.

cards.plain: Hormozi's Scaling Roadmap splits a company into 10 stages by number of people. Each stage has a "bottom line" problem; you graduate by solving that one problem, not by doing everything at once. He says to study only your stage, plus one before and one after.
cards.analogy: Tennis: a kid at Red ball doesn't learn kick serves. Red → Orange → Green is a sequence; skipping a colour makes them worse, not faster. Same with stages.
cards.ex: A gym owner with 3 trainers (Stabilize) reading about board structures (Capitalize) wastes months. His real problem: he's doing every session himself, so the fix is hiring and training trainer #4.
cards.move: You are at **Monetize**. Nothing else matters until one agency pays. Hiring, Multi-site, automations: all later stages. This week: the 150 dials.
cards.trap: Building later-stage stuff (dashboards, SOPs, brand) because it feels like progress. Companies die of indigestion, not starvation.
q: What stage are you in and what is its one job?
Monetize (stage 1): make the first sale, a paying agency.
Why only study 3 stages?
Everything else is premature; it eats focus from the one problem that graduates you.

cards.hook: At any moment **one thing limits your whole business**. Fixing anything else changes nothing.

vis.title: Pipe with one narrow section
steps: only as wide as the pipe
vis.note: Water flows at the speed of the narrowest section. Widen that one; everything else is decoration.

cards.plain: Theory of constraints: a business is a chain. The weakest link sets the output. Find the step where volume drops or stalls, put all effort there, and when it moves, the constraint moves somewhere else.
cards.analogy: A tennis player losing every match on double faults doesn't need a better forehand. Fix the second serve first.
cards.ex: Callers on his hotline blame the economy, media buying, the season. He finds the set call isn't qualifying (no BANT) or the hooks only reach warm buyers. One fix, revenue moves.
cards.move: Your constraint: **owner conversations**. Not the website, not the offer doc, not the app. Count talks per week and push only that number.
cards.trap: Working on what you enjoy and calling it the constraint ("the landing page needs work").
q: How do you find the constraint?
Look for the step where numbers drop or stall, or where you'd still be stuck if everything else doubled.
What happens after you fix it?
The constraint moves to the next step. Find it again.

cards.hook: Before hiring, **write down every 15 minutes for 1–2 weeks**. The patterns show you what to delegate, train or delete.

vis.title: Get out of the bottleneck
steps: red = only me · yellow = train · green = delegate now
scripts + decision boxes ("up to $X you decide")

cards.plain: Owners feel "busy with random things". Logged in 15-minute cells, the random becomes patterns. Most of it is work someone you already pay should do; you keep jumping in because training feels slower than doing it.
cards.analogy: A coach who picks up every ball himself never runs a real drill. Teach the kids to collect balls once; you get 10 minutes back every session forever.
cards.ex: A hunting-store owner at $6.5M worked 80 h/week. Time study → customer service was his 24-year-old rep's job (needs a script), purchasing needed a written decision tree ("within 6% of last year, else send this email"). Then hire one person for the rest.
cards.move: Run a 1-week time study now, while it's just you: it shows how much time actually goes to dials vs "admin". Later, it becomes the job description of your first hire.
cards.trap: Hiring 3 people you won't train instead of training 1 well. And "decide what's best" with no decision box.
cards.memo: **"Log it, colour it, train it, then hire."**
q: What's a decision box?
The limits within which someone decides alone (e.g. up to $X; try fixes 1, 2, 3 before calling me).
Why is jumping in "lazy"?
It's short-term relief that costs you forever; training costs more once and frees you permanently.
clip: Train, don't jump in: time study and decision boxes
Fred vs William: a business that runs without you

cards.hook: Your first hire buys back the hours where you **earn the most**, so you can spend them selling.

a: Someone to sell for you before you can sell
Hire, then figure out the job
b: Job = the green rows of your time study

cards.plain: Trade money for time only when the time you free is worth more than the salary. The hire should take the repeatable work you've already proven, so you go back to the money-making activity.
cards.analogy: A tennis club owner hires a coach for the 4–6 pm kids' sessions so he can sell memberships at the desk. Not a "manager".
cards.ex: Gym couple on his live: hire for the afternoon sessions so the owner can sell. Rule of thumb from his lives: the hire must free time that turns into more revenue than they cost.
cards.move: Not yet. After ~3 paying agencies, the first hire is likely a caregiver sourcer/screener so you stay on the phone with owners.
cards.trap: Hiring a salesperson before you've proven the script yourself. Then you don't know whether the person or the process failed.
cards.memo: **"Hire the hours, keep the money work."**
q: When does a hire make sense?
When the hours it frees produce more than its cost, and the task is already proven and repeatable.

cards.hook: If the business **dies when you take a month off**, you own a job, not a business.

vis.title: What buyers pay for (rough idea)
vis.note: Illustrative: the less it depends on you, the more it's worth.

cards.plain: Enterprise value comes from systems, people and customers that keep producing without you. The tests he uses: can someone do 80% as well as you on a task? Does it keep running for 3 months without you?
cards.analogy: A tennis academy where only the head coach can teach is a private coach with a sign. One where every coach runs the same drills is an academy.
cards.ex: Owner-operator "Fred" does everything; hands-off "William" built roles and training. Same revenue, very different sale price.
cards.move: Far later. But build habits now: write each process once (dial script, screening checklist) so a hire can copy it.
cards.trap: Waiting for someone to be 100% as good as you. 80% is the bar.
cards.memo: **"80% as good is good enough to hand off."**
q: What's the 80% test?
If someone can do a task 80% as well as you, hand it off.

cards.t: Prioritize: niche down to your best customer
cards.hook: Stage 4's problem is **trying to be everything to everyone**. The fix: serve the customers who are easiest to help and pay the most.
cards.plain: At first, take anyone with a card. Once you have data, find the customers who get results fastest, stay longest and pay most, then build everything around them: one message, one offer, one channel.
cards.analogy: A coach who teaches toddlers, juniors, adults and seniors is mediocre at all four; the junior-academy coach becomes the best in town.
cards.ex: "We help doctors get patients using podcasts": one thing for many, cut once, sell twice (DOAC).
cards.move: Your routing question ("how many caregivers do you hire in a normal month?") is the niche filter. Track which answers turn into paying agencies.
cards.trap: Niching before you have data, or never niching because "anyone could use this".
q: When do you niche down?
After you have enough customers to see which ones are easiest and pay most (~$1–3M or stage 4).

cards.hook: Start at the top: **expensive, done-for-you, few clients**. Then build cheaper versions down the pyramid.

vis.title: Sales ↔ fulfilment
rungs: course: hard to sell, easy to deliver
expensive, easy to sell, hard to deliver
vis.note: Tesla: Roadster (~$100k) → Model S → Model 3 (~$30k). The expensive version funds and proves the cheap one.

cards.plain: Few expensive clients teach you the most, pay for the learning, and anchor future prices. Add one or two zeros to your price and list what you'd have to do to be worth it.
cards.analogy: Private lessons first, then group clinics, then a video course for the masses.
cards.ex: "That's not scalable." "You're broke; you can just make money." You only need five clients at $100k (DOAC).
cards.move: Caregiver Bench is done-for-you by design. Don't build courses or software now; serve 5 agencies like they're your only five.
cards.trap: Starting with the cheap scalable product because it "scales".
q: Why start expensive?
Better customers, more learning per client, cash, and a high price anchor.
clip: Very expensive to few, or cheap to all

cards.hook: Design the business as **steps that must happen**, not job titles. Then give each step to a person, a tool or an agent.
cards.plain: Roles become junk drawers. A workflow shows every step, who owns it and where it breaks. In 2026 he sees the opportunity in people-heavy businesses run as agent workflows.
cards.analogy: A drill: feed, hit, recover, next. Each step has an owner; nobody is "in charge of tennis".
cards.ex: Agency owner who was the bottleneck: build an intake that spins up assets automatically, then script sales so a non-expert closes (Feb 2026 hotline).
cards.move: Write your delivery workflow as 6 boxes (like the diagram) this week. That's the SOP, the hiring plan and the automation map in one.
cards.trap: Hiring a "head of ops" with no defined workflow.
q: Why are roles risky?
They become junk drawers; workflows make every step visible and assignable.

cards.hook: Culture = **what you define, demonstrate, correct and praise**, until the team does it to each other.
cards.plain: "Be more professional" means nothing. Define it as things you can see or hear. Pair every KPI with a quality metric. Rules without enforcement are suggestions.
cards.analogy: "Good footwork" = split step before every shot. Now a kid can do it and you can check it.
cards.ex: Lawn care: speed KPI paired with quality: cut a corner, redo it on your own time and lose that day's bonus.
cards.move: When you hire caregivers or a sourcer: write "good" as 5 observable behaviours (reply within 1 hour, confirm the shift the night before…).
cards.trap: Vague feedback ("be curious") that people must translate and get wrong.
cards.memo: **"If I can't see it, it's not defined."**
q: What's a paired metric?
A second metric that stops gaming the first (speed + quality).
When is culture "there"?
When people praise each other publicly and correct each other privately.

cards.t: Speed of decisions = speed of the company
cards.hook: A company moves as fast as its decisions. **Decide, act, learn**; slow "maybe" is the most expensive answer.
cards.plain: Unmade decisions are the heaviest thing you carry. Most are reversible; make them quickly and use feedback. Remove before you add.
cards.analogy: Hesitating on an approach shot: half in, half out, you lose the point either way.
cards.ex: "Burn the boats" and "remove first" (Jul 2026 live).
cards.move: Plan changes only happen at the Sunday review; inside the week, decide in minutes using the "does it make $20k more likely?" test.
cards.trap: Researching a decision that changes nothing about your day.
q: What do you do before adding something new?
Remove something first.

cards.hook: Value goes **up** with the dream and the belief it will work, and **down** with waiting and effort.

vis.title: Value equation
bottom: what they must do or give up
vis.note: Green boxes you push up. Red boxes you push toward zero. Shrinking the bottom is usually cheaper than growing the top.

cards.plain: People don't buy products; they buy a result. Make the result bigger, make them more sure they'll get it (proof, guarantees), make it faster, and make it easier. Each change raises what they'll happily pay.
cards.analogy: Tennis lessons: "Your kid will rally with a friend in 6 weeks (dream, fast), 9 of 10 kids do (likelihood), I bring rackets and pick them up from school (no effort)." Same lessons, 2× the price.
cards.ex: Swim school on his hotline: from $100/month to "12 sessions, your kid floats, or I keep teaching free": a defined result + guarantee, priced $600 up front.
cards.move: Caregiver Bench: dream = shifts covered; likelihood = Show-Up Guarantee + Stay-or-Replace 90; time = first caregiver within days; effort = you do sourcing and screening, they just interview. Say all four on every call.
cards.trap: Only adding features (the top) and ignoring time and effort (the bottom), which buyers feel most.
q: Which two parts go on the bottom?
Time delay and effort & sacrifice.
Cheapest way to raise value?
Usually cut time and effort, not add more stuff.

cards.hook: Make an offer **so good people feel stupid saying no**, by solving every problem around the outcome.
cards.plain: Write down every obstacle between the buyer and the result. Each obstacle becomes a solution. Pick how you'll deliver each, cut what costs a lot and adds little, and stack the rest into one package.
cards.analogy: A racket stringer who also re-grips, checks tension monthly, and loans a racket while yours is being strung. Same core service, impossible to compare on price.
cards.ex: Gym: "lose 20 lbs in 6 weeks" + meal plan + weekly weigh-ins + accountability calls + supplements, money back if you hit every session.
cards.move: Agency owner problems: no applicants, no-shows, quitting in month one, no time to screen. Your answers: bench of screened caregivers, Show-Up Guarantee, 90-Day Stay-or-Replace, you do the screening. That's your stack.
cards.trap: Adding bonuses that cost you a lot of time but the buyer barely values.
cards.memo: **"Every problem → a solution → stack the best."**
q: Step after listing problems?
Turn each problem into a solution, then choose delivery vehicles, then trim and stack.

cards.hook: A great offer to a bad market loses to an average offer to a **starving crowd**.
cards.plain: Before the offer, choose who you sell to. Pain, money, reachability and growth. Then niche down until your message sounds written for them.
cards.analogy: Selling tennis lessons in a town with no courts vs next to a club with a waiting list. Same coach, different result.
cards.ex: Private-pay home care agencies in Naples: aging rich population (growing, money), chronic caregiver shortage (pain), owners listed and callable (targetable).
cards.move: Your market checks all four. That's why switching niches now would be a mistake; push volume instead.
cards.trap: Picking a market because it's "interesting", then wondering why nobody buys.
q: The 4 market criteria?
Massive pain, purchasing power, easy to target, growing.
clip: The 4 signs of a good market

cards.t: Charge premium: the virtuous cycle of price
cards.hook: Higher price → more money to deliver better → better results → **more proof → you can charge more**.

vis.title: Close rate tells you the price (his rule of thumb)

cards.plain: Cheap prices attract the worst customers and leave no money to delivery. A premium price funds a better service and better customers. If almost everyone says yes, your price is too low.
cards.analogy: The coach charging double gets families who show up every week and practise; the cheap coach gets cancellations.
cards.ex: His first $6,000 sale came from naming a price he hoped they'd refuse. Lawn care company closing 70%: raise the price.
cards.move: Priority Bench is $2,500 / 4 weeks incl. 2 working caregivers. Anchor it against recruiters ($4,800–8,000 a hire). Don't discount. Free or full price, never in between.
cards.trap: Discounting to "get started". Discounts train buyers to wait and squeeze your delivery budget.
cards.memo: **"If they all say yes, you said a small number."**
q: Closing 80%+ means?
Underpriced, often 3–4×.
Why premium helps delivery?
More margin = more resources = better results = more proof.
clip: The price you hope they refuse

cards.hook: A guarantee moves the risk from the buyer to you, and **usually brings in far more than it costs**.

vis.title: 4 kinds
items: results if they do X (best for services)
performance pricing: pay when it works

cards.plain: Fear of losing is bigger than desire to gain. Take away the loss and more people buy. Do the maths: if it triples sales and a few ask for refunds, you win. Conditional guarantees tie the promise to their effort.
cards.analogy: "If your kid comes to all 12 lessons and still can't rally, I teach for free until they can."
cards.ex: Swim school: attend all sessions → kid floats, or free lessons until they do. Webinar guarantees on his live: guarantee traffic, leads or sales, whatever you can control.
cards.move: You already have two: Show-Up Guarantee (replacement in 24h) and 90-Day Stay-or-Replace. Say them early and plainly; they're the "likelihood" part of value.
cards.trap: Hiding the guarantee in fine print. If you have it, lead with it.
q: Which guarantee type fits services best?
Conditional: the result if they do their part.

cards.hook: **Scarcity = limited quantity. Urgency = limited time.** Both make "later" more expensive than "now".
cards.plain: People delay. Real limits give them a reason to act now. Use only true limits; fake scarcity destroys trust.
cards.analogy: "Saturday group has 1 spot left" fills it faster than "we have groups".
cards.ex: Mylett episode: cutting supply is real scarcity; it also lets you raise price.
cards.move: Use your real ones: max 2 Priority members per town area; Founding 5 get a 12-month price lock. "I can only take one more agency in Bonita Springs."
cards.trap: Invented deadlines. Owners talk to each other.
q: Difference scarcity vs urgency?
Scarcity limits quantity; urgency limits time.
clip: Scarcity = cut supply · scarcity vs urgency

cards.hook: Bonuses should be **worth more than the core offer** together and solve the next problem the buyer will hit.
cards.plain: Offer the core thing, then add bonuses one by one, each with a name, a value and the problem it solves. Each bonus answers a "but what about…" before they say it.
cards.analogy: Racket + free first restring + grip + 1 lesson on serve: the racket price suddenly looks small.
cards.ex: Membership launch on his hotline: annual plan gets 1–2 exclusive bonuses; monthly gets none, so most choose annual.
cards.move: Possible bonuses: Monday Bench Bulletin (free leads list of available caregivers), an onboarding checklist for new caregivers, a no-show text template. Name them.
cards.trap: Bonuses that are just more of the same thing.
q: What should each bonus do?
Solve a specific next problem / objection, with a name and value.
clip: Show the parts as bonuses (5/10 → 10/10 offer)

cards.hook: A good name tells the right person **what they get, how fast, in what form**.
cards.plain: Use 3–5 of the five pieces. The name should make the right buyer think "that's for me" in one read.
cards.analogy: "Summer Serve Bootcamp: kids 8–12 hit their first serve in 5 days" vs "tennis lessons".
cards.ex: "First Hire Free: a 30-day trial for Collier home care agencies" uses Magnetic reason, Avatar, Time, Container.
cards.move: Use the name in the first 20 seconds of the call and in every text.
cards.trap: Clever names that need explaining.
q: What does the C in MAGIC stand for?
Complete with a container word (program, trial, challenge…).
cards.clipNote: Alex Hormozi in the course lesson closest to this idea ("Grand Slam Offer").

cards.t: Category of one (escape the commodity trap)
cards.hook: If buyers can compare you line by line, **they compare on price**. Make an offer that has no comparison.

b: screened bench + show-up guarantee + replace in 24h

cards.plain: Lowering price has a floor (zero, a race to failure). Raising value has no ceiling. Stack unique elements so the offer becomes its own category.
cards.analogy: "Tennis lessons" vs "the 6-week rally program with video analysis and a guarantee".
cards.ex: Course: the $50,000 burger: price is relative to the buyer; sell dollars at a discount.
cards.move: Never say "we're like a staffing agency but…". Say what nobody else does: guarantee, 24h replacement, pay when they work.
cards.trap: Describing yourself with your competitors' words.
q: Floor of competing on price?
Zero: a race to failure.

cards.hook: Tiers should jump **about 5× in price**. +20% tiers just confuse people.

vis.title: A clean ladder
vis.note: Wealth is lopsided (top 1% hold ~30%), so a premium tier ~5× up catches buyers worth far more.

cards.plain: Buyers differ hugely in what they can pay. Big jumps between tiers let each buyer self-select; small jumps make tiers look the same.
cards.analogy: Group class, semi-private, private: each step clearly more.
cards.ex: Interior designer's tiers were ~20% apart: undifferentiated. Fix: one core price + a tiny retainer to stay in their life (Feb 2026 hotline).
cards.move: Present Multi-site first (anchor), then Priority Bench, then Pay When They Work only after a no.
cards.trap: Three tiers with nearly the same price.
q: Why ~5× jumps?
Clear self-selection; wealth is lopsided so the top tier captures big buyers.

cards.t: Free or full price, never a discount
cards.hook: Discounts below ~50% don't change behaviour; they just cost you. **Give free (to start) or charge full.**
cards.plain: When someone hesitates, add value or change terms, never cut the price of the core offer. If you want a smaller price, splinter off a smaller thing.
cards.analogy: Don't discount the term; offer one free trial class.
cards.ex: Course: never discount the core offer; splinter off one piece. Never negotiate on price; stay a helpful guide.
cards.move: Your rule already: free (First Hire Free) or full price. Founding 5 get a price lock, not a discount.
cards.trap: "Just this once" discounts that become the price.
q: Alternative to discounting?
Change terms (payment plan, trial) or remove a piece for a smaller price.
cards.clipNote: Alex Hormozi in the course lesson closest to this idea ("Charge premium: the virtuous cycle of price").

cards.hook: Sell a **defined outcome with an end** (12 sessions, 6 weeks), not open-ended month-to-month. Then pitch the next phase halfway.

steps: what they paid rolls into the bigger offer

cards.plain: Defined outcomes are easier to buy and value; they collect more cash up front, which fixes CAC payback.
cards.analogy: "Rally in 6 weeks" sells better than "$100 a month for lessons".
cards.ex: Swim school: $600 for 12 sessions, then a 6-phase program at halfway with the $600 credited. PT gym: €600 six-week onboarding, credit toward the year.
cards.move: First Hire Free is your defined front end (30 days, one open case). Day 25 = halfway pitch for Priority Bench.
cards.trap: Waiting until the end to pitch the next step.
q: When do you pitch the back end?
Halfway, not at the end.
clip: PT gym: price the front end

cards.hook: Price is only big or small **compared to something**. Pick the comparison.

vis.title: What an owner compares you to

cards.plain: Without an anchor, buyers compare you to zero. Name the real alternative: a recruiter, a lost client, their own unpaid hours.
cards.analogy: A $35k program sounds huge until a year of college costs ~$38k.
cards.ex: Career program on his hotline: priced against a year of college; pitched halfway; half now, half when the job lands.
cards.move: Always say the recruiter number before your price: "recruiters charge $4,800–8,000 per hire…"
cards.trap: Saying your price before giving a comparison.
q: Your anchor?
Recruiter fees of $4,800–8,000 per hire.

cards.hook: There are only **4 ways** to let people know: talk to people you know, talk to strangers, post content, run ads.

vis.title: Who you reach × how
cells: texts, calls, DMs to people who know you
pay to reach strangers at scale
vis.note: Highlighted = where you live: cold outreach. Later, ads and content scale it.

cards.plain: Every lead in history came from one of these. You don't need all four; you need one done at volume until it works, then add the next.
cards.analogy: Getting tennis students: tell friends (warm), flyers at schools (cold), videos of kids improving (content), Facebook ads (paid).
cards.ex: Need money tomorrow? Warm outreach (Mylett). Most of his hotline callers are stuck on one channel at low volume.
cards.move: Your channel is **cold outreach** (dials). Next, when it converts: content (short videos about caregiver hiring) and lead getters (referral partners).
cards.trap: Doing all four at 10% each. Pick one, do 100% volume.
q: The Core Four?
Warm outreach, cold outreach, content, paid ads.

cards.hook: Do **100 primary actions a day for 100 days**. Volume negates luck.

vis.title: The maths of volume
vis.note: Most people get a first customer by week three when they actually hit the number.

cards.plain: 100 dials, 100 DMs, 100 minutes of content, or $100 a day of ads. Every day. The number removes "did I do enough?" and the reps make you good.
cards.analogy: Hitting 100 serves a day for 100 days. Nobody stays bad at serving after 10,000 serves.
cards.ex: His rule-of-thumb live: feast-or-famine businesses stop being feast-or-famine when the daily number never drops to zero.
cards.move: Your commitment is 150 dials a week (Mon 5 · Tue 50 · Wed 5 · Thu 70 · Fri 20). Minimum day = 10 dials + 25 min BAC, never zero. That's your version.
cards.trap: Counting "worked on outreach" instead of a number. If you can't count it, it didn't happen.
cards.memo: **"100 × 100: count it or it didn't happen."**
q: What counts as a primary action?
The core lead action itself: a dial, a DM, a post, ad spend; not "planning outreach".

cards.hook: Give away a **complete solution to a narrow problem**, one that reveals the next problem you sell.

vis.title: How a lead magnet works
steps: "I need them screened and showing up"

cards.plain: It must actually help (so they trust you) and be quick to consume. Three types: reveal a problem, a sample/trial, or one step of a multi-step process.
cards.analogy: A free 15-minute serve check that shows the kid's toss is the problem. The fix is the lesson package.
cards.ex: Don't call it an "audit": say "we'll find you 7 revenue opportunities in 30 days" (SEO caller). Five free 1:1 calls as a lead magnet for a data consultancy.
cards.move: Your magnets for "not now" owners: Hiring Snapshot + Monday Bench Bulletin. Offer them to every no; that's how no becomes later.
cards.trap: Boring names ("free audit") and magnets that solve the whole problem so nothing is left to sell.
q: 3 types of lead magnet?
Reveal a problem, a sample/trial, one step of a multi-step process.
clip: Lead magnet naming + content is the lead magnet

cards.hook: Every ad or post: **hook** their attention, **retain** it, **reward** them with value. Hooks decide who even hears you.

vis.title: Awareness (Schwartz) ↔ how wide your hook is
rows: curiosity: "losing $ every week because of one thing"
vis.note: Hooks only for the bottom = small audience, ads cap out. Go up the funnel to reach more.

cards.plain: Hook: the first seconds or line. Retain: keep them with story or steps. Reward: they leave better off. If your ads stop scaling, your hooks only speak to people who already know your type of offer.
cards.analogy: A rally: serve (hook), keep the ball in play (retain), win the point (reward).
cards.ex: Agency spending $5k/day hit a ceiling: the hooks only talked to buyers who already knew ManyChat. Wider hooks + a lighter ask unlocked more reach.
cards.move: Your phone opener is a hook. Lead with the owner's pain (no-shows, open shifts) before your service.
cards.trap: Leading with your product name to people who don't know they have the problem.
q: Why do ads cap out?
Hooks only fit most-aware buyers; widen them to less-aware levels.

cards.hook: Call a new lead **within 5 minutes**. Slow follow-up can roughly 4× your real cost per customer.

vis.title: Contact rate falls with delay (direction, not exact)

cards.plain: Interest decays fast. The person who asked is warmest right now; every hour they cool and talk to competitors.
cards.analogy: Return a short ball before the opponent recovers position.
cards.ex: Rule-of-thumb live: 5-minute speed to lead, book calls same or next day, max ~4 days out.
cards.move: When an owner texts back or asks for info: answer immediately, book the call for today or tomorrow.
cards.trap: "I'll reply in the evening batch."
q: Target time to contact a new lead?
Under 5 minutes.

cards.t: Lead getters: referrals, affiliates, agencies, employees
cards.hook: After you can get leads yourself, get **other people to get them for you**.

items: people you pay to do outreach
partners paid per result (careful: legal lines)

cards.plain: Lead getters multiply the Core Four. Referrals come from great results + asking; affiliates from people who already have your customers.
cards.analogy: A club pro sending you private students.
cards.ex: "Fastest leads": go to whoever already has your customers one or two decisions before you and make a referral deal.
cards.move: Legal line: you can't pay per family/client/lead (Florida Patient Brokering Act). Ask owners for intros to other owners instead; Founding 5 includes 2 intros.
cards.trap: Paying for referrals in a regulated industry without checking the law.
cards.memo: **"Your customers' neighbours are your next customers."**
q: What's your legal limit here?
Never pay per family/client/lead/referral; ask for intros instead.
clip: Fastest leads: who has your customers first

cards.hook: When stuck: first do **more** of what you do, then do it **better**, only then try something **new**.

vis.title: The order
steps: only when more & better are maxed

cards.plain: Most people switch strategies before the first one had a fair test. More is the cheapest test; better comes from the data volume gives you; new is the last resort.
cards.analogy: Not winning matches? Play more matches before changing your grip.
cards.ex: His hotline: "more" has the best risk-adjusted return; a realtor doing 5 live tours a week instead of 2 could roughly quadruple business.
cards.move: Before any new channel or offer idea: are you at 150 dials/week for 4 weeks straight? If not, the answer is more.
cards.trap: "New" disguised as strategy because more is boring.
q: What comes before "new"?
More, then better.
clip: Commit to volume, then get better

cards.hook: Fastest money: message people who know you. **Acknowledge, Compliment, Ask** ("do you know anyone who…?").
cards.plain: Ask for referrals, not purchases. People help when they don't feel sold. Go through your whole contact list.
cards.analogy: Asking parents of your students if their friends' kids want a spot.
cards.ex: Need money tomorrow? Warm outreach (Mylett episode).
cards.move: Text everyone you know in Florida/US healthcare or with family there: "do you know a home care agency owner?" One intro beats 50 cold dials.
cards.trap: Asking friends to buy instead of asking who they know.
q: What do you ask for in warm outreach?
Who they know (a referral), not a purchase.

cards.t: Content: give the secrets, harvest with ads
cards.hook: Give away the **what and why**; people pay for the **how-done-for-them**. Content builds goodwill, ads harvest it.
cards.plain: Educate, don't entertain, if you're a business. Make content for the exact buyer; views from the wrong people don't count. Capture your real work rather than inventing content.
cards.analogy: Free tennis tips on Instagram fill your private lesson slots.
cards.ex: Gym Launch ads underperformed 12 weeks after he stopped gym content: 78% of buyers had watched 2+ long videos first.
cards.move: Later channel: 1 short video a day answering an owner question ("how to stop caregiver no-shows"). Film real calls' lessons, not skits.
cards.trap: Judging content by views instead of the right people's responses.
q: Why did his ads drop at Gym Launch?
He stopped making gym content; ads were harvesting goodwill content built.
clip: Social media is now interest media

cards.hook: Most creators never ask. Put a clear ask in **5 spots**: bio, pinned comment, first description line, community post, in-video at ⅓.
cards.plain: Conversions happen in conversations. Each ask is cheap; not asking is the most expensive mistake.
cards.analogy: Telling every parent at the end of class "Saturday group has 2 spots".
cards.ex: Fitness coach with daily videos and 5–10 leads/month: add CTAs in all five spots, push to DMs or a calendar.
cards.move: When you post, every post ends with one ask: "agency owners: text me 'bench' for this week's available caregivers".
cards.trap: Long, repeated CTAs that kill retention.
q: Where's the in-video ask?
About a third of the way through.
clip: Where to put your calls to action

cards.hook: If a stranger can't say what you do after one sentence, **that's your lead problem**.

b: "I take photos that get you interviews"
"I find screened caregivers for home care agencies in Naples"

cards.plain: Confused people don't buy or refer. Say who it's for and what they get in plain words.
cards.analogy: "Serve clinic for kids 8–12" vs "Holistic Racket Development".
cards.ex: Caller with a "science-based executive clarity service": he couldn't tell what it was. Fix the message first.
cards.move: Test your one-liner on someone outside the industry; if they can repeat it, use it.
cards.trap: Jargon to sound bigger.
q: The 5-year-old test?
Explain it so a child could repeat it.

cards.hook: More output → more prospects, almost **linearly**. 100× the volume, roughly 100× the leads.
cards.plain: People try to out-smart the work. In practice, consistent volume with the right content scales predictably (1 in 10 shorts outperforms; the maths is known).
cards.analogy: More serves practised = more aces. No shortcut.
cards.ex: Dave Ramsey: hours a day for 40 years. Consistency is wildly underestimated.
cards.move: Same law for dials: 150/week now; when it converts, the next lever is more dials, not a new channel.
cards.trap: Looking for the trick instead of the number.
cards.memo: **"Double the input, roughly double the output."**
q: What's the edge most people underestimate?
Consistency.

cards.hook: Every business is three numbers: **what a customer costs (CAC), what they're worth (gross profit), and how fast you get paid back.**

vis.title: Get customers cheap · make lots per customer · fast
steps: total sales & marketing cost ÷ new customers

cards.plain: Lower CAC, higher gross profit, faster payback. That's it. Every tactic in Money Models moves one of these three.
cards.analogy: A tennis tournament: entry fee (CAC), prize money (gross profit), and whether the prize pays before the next entry fee is due (payback).
cards.ex: His meal business: $100 CAC, "$500 lifetime revenue" looked 5:1, but at 20% margin it was ~$100 lifetime profit. Losing money. He shut meals down; supplements made 95% of profit.
cards.move: Track yours from the first agency: CAC = your hours on dials × value + any costs ÷ agencies signed; gross profit = fee − sourcing/screening cost; payback in days.
cards.trap: Using revenue instead of gross profit. Revenue lies.
q: Why gross profit not revenue?
Revenue ignores delivery cost; you can grow revenue and lose money.
clip: LTV:CAC by humans in the loop

cards.hook: A customer must bring at least **3× their acquisition cost in lifetime gross profit**, more if humans are in the loop.

vis.title: Ratio needed (his rule of thumb)
vis.note: Each human step in selling or delivery adds cost and risk, so you need more margin of safety.

cards.plain: LTGP = gross profit per month × months they stay. Divide by CAC. Below 3:1 you're one bad month from trouble. Services with people in sales and delivery need more.
cards.analogy: A club only survives if a member's yearly fees cover far more than what it cost to sign them up and coach them.
cards.ex: Gym Launch ran near 100:1 at its peak. CAC tends to be similar across an industry; the winner is whoever's customer is worth more.
cards.move: One Priority agency at ~$2,500/4 weeks, staying 12 months ≈ 13 payments. Even at 50% gross margin that's ~$16k LTGP. Your CAC is mostly your time: the ratio is huge if they stay. Retention is the whole game.
cards.trap: Celebrating a sale that churns in month 2.
q: How do you compute LTGP?
Monthly gross profit × average months retained.

cards.hook: For services, aim for **80% gross margin**. 70% vs 80% looks close but changes everything.

vis.title: Profit per $1,000 sale after a $500 CAC
vis.note: The gap widens once you pay for acquisition. Margin is the fuel for ads, people and guarantees.

cards.plain: Gross margin = (price − delivery cost) ÷ price. Services have no inventory, so low margin means you're underpriced or delivering inefficiently.
cards.analogy: A coach charging $30 a lesson and paying $25 for the court has nothing left to grow.
cards.ex: His live: 70% vs 80% vs 90% margin means very different money left for acquisition and growth.
cards.move: Know your delivery cost per agency (sourcing ads, your screening hours, texts/phone). Price so it's ≤ 20% of the fee.
cards.trap: Ignoring your own time as a cost.
q: Gross margin formula?
(price − cost to deliver) ÷ price.

cards.hook: If a customer pays back their CAC **within 30 days**, every customer funds the next. Money stops being your limit.

vis.title: Client-financed acquisition levels
rungs: lifetime gross profit > CAC (you wait months)
30-day gross profit > CAC (never use your own money)

cards.plain: Credit cards give ~30 days interest-free. If customers repay acquisition cost inside that window, you can grow as fast as you can find buyers.
cards.analogy: A tournament where the prize arrives before the next entry fee is due: you can enter every week.
cards.ex: Cash in 48 hours (his order): existing customers prepay, past customers win-back, attraction offer to leads.
cards.move: The Day-25 results call sells the plan before day 30, so the first payment lands quickly. Ask for prepay of 4 weeks up front.
cards.trap: Long free trials with payment at the end, stretching payback.
q: Level 3 means?
30-day gross profit > 2× CAC: unlimited growth from cash.

cards.hook: "Free brings broke people" is a myth. **Free creates flow; then you monetise and add friction.**
cards.plain: Free offers get cheaper leads with similar close rates. Too many bad leads is a good problem: then you add questions and filters.
cards.analogy: A free kids' tennis day fills the court; you sell the term to families whose kids loved it.
cards.ex: His hotline: adding friction raised the % qualified and lowered the absolute number; mission accomplished, then push more volume at the top.
cards.move: First Hire Free is exactly this. Don't add hoops until you have more trials than you can handle.
cards.trap: Adding friction before you have flow.
q: When do you add friction?
Only after you have more flow than you can serve.

cards.hook: The first offer gets people in the door **and pays for itself**, so acquisition is funded by the buyer.

vis.title: Six attraction offers
items: hit the goal, get it back
cheap version beside premium; most pick premium
Pay less now or more later
free if they show up / take action

cards.plain: An attraction offer lowers the risk to start. Each type uses a different lever: a bet on success, a prize, a contrast, a bundle, a trial or a behaviour.
cards.analogy: "Bring a friend, first month free for both" (Buy X get Y).
cards.ex: Giveaway on his hotline: everyone applies for the grand prize; you sell the second-place prize to the rest.
cards.move: First Hire Free = a "pay later / free with consumption" mix: agency agrees to reply in 24h and interview in 72h; miss twice and it ends.
cards.trap: Attraction offers with no next offer behind them.
cards.memo: **"Get them in cheap, pay for it with what comes next."**
q: Name 3 attraction offers.
Win your money back, giveaway, decoy, buy X get Y, pay less now or more later, free with consumption.

cards.hook: Sell the next thing **at the moment they want it most**: right after the yes, after the first win, halfway through.

vis.title: 4 upsells
items: "you can't have X without Y" (fries with the burger)
unsell, prescribe, A/B choice, card on file
show the 5–10× option first, then the main one
credit what they paid toward a bigger offer

cards.plain: The best time to sell is when they just decided to buy or just got a result. Five moments: immediately, next step (24–72h), after the first win, halfway, last chance.
cards.analogy: The kid just hit their first rally: that's when parents buy the term, not on day one.
cards.ex: Swim school: halfway through the 12 sessions, pitch the 6-phase program and credit the $600.
cards.move: Day-25 results call = your upsell moment. Anchor: present Multi-site ($6,000) first, then Priority Bench ($2,500) looks right.
cards.trap: Upselling before the first win.
q: What is an anchor upsell?
Show a much bigger option first (5–10×), then the main offer feels reasonable.
clip: Defined front end + halfway back end

cards.hook: When they say no to price, **never sell the same thing for less**. Change the terms or remove something.

vis.title: Order
steps: free if they act, fees if not
remove value for a lower price

cards.plain: A discount teaches people to say no. Instead: spread payments, offer a trial with conditions, or remove a piece (fewer caregivers, no guarantee).
cards.analogy: Can't afford the weekly group? Offer every other week, not the same weekly group cheaper.
cards.ex: Course: "you choose the terms" → payment plan; then trial with penalty; then feature downsell.
cards.move: Your downsell is Pay When They Work: $1,500 per caregiver who works ($2,000 hard case). Only after a no to Priority Bench.
cards.trap: "Okay, $1,800 then." Never.
q: Your downsell?
Pay When They Work, only after a no.

cards.hook: Recurring revenue stacks: **keep clients past month 6** and churn usually drops sharply.

vis.title: Same 10 new clients a month, after 12 months
vis.note: Illustrative arithmetic: lower churn = much bigger base from the same selling.

cards.plain: Revenue retention sets the ceiling of any business. Focus the first months on activation and results; offer a bonus worth more than the first payment; bill every 4 weeks; waived setup fee for a 12-month commitment.
cards.analogy: A tennis academy grows by keeping kids for years, not by signing new ones every month.
cards.ex: Agency with 10% monthly churn resells ~70% of its revenue every year. Across services, past month six, churn often falls under ~2%.
cards.move: Your MRR goal ($20k) dies with churn. Day-25 call, guarantee, and quick replacements are retention tools. Bill every 4 weeks (13 cycles a year).
cards.trap: Chasing new sales while old clients quietly leave.
q: Why bill every 4 weeks?
13 cycles a year instead of 12: an extra month of revenue.

cards.hook: Charge up front; **they earn it back by hitting the goal**. Your cash comes in, their motivation goes up.
cards.plain: The point isn't that they win; it's that they start and show up. Many roll the money into the next offer instead of taking it back.
cards.analogy: "Come to all 12 sessions and the term is free."
cards.ex: PT gym: 6-week €600, give a goal, money back if they hit it, pitch the year halfway and credit the €600.
cards.move: Not a fit for agencies (B2B). Keep it as a pattern for your tennis groups.
cards.trap: Making the goal so hard nobody tries, or so easy you refund everyone.
q: What's the real purpose?
Getting them to start and show up.

cards.t: Pay less now or pay more later
cards.hook: Offer a **free trial with the card on file** (or a small fee now vs bigger later). Most stay; ~10% cancel.

b: full price on day 30 if they stay

cards.plain: Removing the first payment removes the fear. The card on file turns "maybe later" into "yes unless I cancel".
cards.analogy: "First month free, then $80, cancel anytime."
cards.ex: Course: Pay Less Now or Pay More Later, card on file, about 10% cancel.
cards.move: First Hire Free: card on file; Priority Bench starts at day 30 only if a caregiver worked. Always get the card on day 1.
cards.trap: Free trials without a card: they just disappear.
q: What makes the trial convert?
Card on file so continuing is the default.
lesson: Pay Less Now or Pay More Later
cards.clipNote: Alex Hormozi in the course lesson closest to this idea ("Annual first, then monthly").

cards.hook: Add a **3% processing fee and waive it** for bank payment (ACH). Pure profit, fewer failed payments.
cards.plain: Lost cards and declines cause a lot of churn. A second payment method fixes it; the fee motivates the switch. Waived setup fees can also reward 12-month commitments.
cards.analogy: Membership: pay by direct debit and skip the card fee.
cards.ex: Course: he's never seen the 3% fee cost a sale.
cards.move: When you bill agencies: card with 3% or ACH free. Waive any setup in exchange for 12 months later on (Multi-site).
cards.trap: Ignoring involuntary churn (failed cards).
q: Why ACH?
Bank accounts change less than cards, rarely decline, cost less.
cards.clipNote: Alex Hormozi in the course lesson closest to this idea ("Attraction offers").

cards.hook: Credit everything they've paid toward an offer **~4× bigger**. It feels like a gift; you win the bigger sale.
cards.plain: Sunk cost works for you: "you've already invested X, let's make it count toward the full program".
cards.analogy: Trial class fee credited to the term.
cards.ex: Virtual event: after the goal, roll the $1k ticket credit into the $2k/yr community.
cards.move: First Hire Free has no payment to roll. Later: credit Pay When They Work fees toward the first Priority Bench period.
cards.trap: Crediting toward something not much bigger.
q: How big should the target offer be?
About 4× (or more) the credited amount.

cards.hook: Add up what you'll **save or make them**, and charge a slice of that, not your hours.
cards.plain: Hourly billing caps your income and makes clients watch the clock. Price on the result; ~30% of measured value is a common ceiling for result-based services.
cards.analogy: Paid per tournament won, not per hour on court.
cards.ex: Data consultancy billing hourly: find savings in 5 free calls, then charge ~30% of the savings.
cards.move: Your pricing is outcome-linked already (paid when caregivers work). Use the maths on calls: "one open shift costs you $X a week".
cards.trap: Underpricing because the work feels easy to you.
q: Rough ceiling for result-based pricing?
About 30% of the value created.

cards.hook: Sell the **annual (prepaid) option first** with exclusive bonuses; offer monthly afterwards without them.
cards.plain: Prepay fixes 30-day cash and lowers churn. Make the monthly option available but less attractive, never hidden or lied about.
cards.analogy: Season pass with free stringing vs pay-per-class.
cards.ex: $27/mo membership: sell only annual during launch; scoop-up campaign to monthly after.
cards.move: Ask Priority agencies to prepay 3 periods for a bonus (e.g. extra replacement priority). Cash now, less churn.
cards.trap: Leading with monthly because it's easier to say.
q: Why annual first?
Cash up front and lower churn.

cards.hook: Every sales conversation follows **C-L-O-S-E-R**: clarify, label, overview past, sell the vacation, explain concerns, reinforce.

items: what have they tried? why didn't it work? (close the other doors)
the result, not the plane ride
congratulate, set expectations after the yes

cards.plain: You don't pitch first; you get them to say why they need it, admit nothing else worked, then show the result. Objections come last and get handled, then you reinforce so they don't regret.
cards.analogy: A lesson plan: warm-up (clarify), diagnose (label), what drills they did before (overview), show the shot they'll hit (vacation), fix fears (concerns), praise (reinforce).
cards.ex: Swim school on his hotline: "what have you tried? home pool? no time three times a week? So there's no reasonable alternative?" Then the 3 things every kid needs.
cards.move: Map your owner call: C "what made you pick up?"; L "so open shifts and no-shows"; O "agencies and Indeed didn't fix it"; S "shifts covered, you only interview"; E guarantees; R "here's what happens Monday".
cards.trap: Pitching before the overview. You haven't earned it yet.
cards.memo: **C-L-O-S-E-R: Why here, name it, what failed, show result, fears, cheer.**
q: What does O close?
The other doors: what they tried and why it failed, so you are the reasonable choice.
clip: CLOSER on a real call (swim school)

cards.t: Script structure: intro → disco → pitch → close
cards.hook: Frame the call, **diagnose before you prescribe**, pitch in under 2 minutes, then name the price and stay silent.
cards.plain: The agenda gives control. Discovery makes them tell you their pain. The pitch only connects your offer to what they said. Then the price and silence.
cards.analogy: A doctor doesn't prescribe before examining.
cards.ex: Course: recap, label and confirm after discovery, then a short pitch that edifies the expert.
cards.move: Write your 90-second pitch using their own words from discovery. Read it out loud before each block.
cards.trap: Talking more than them in discovery.
q: How long should the pitch be?
About 2 minutes max.
clip: Start your intro sales calls like this

cards.hook: Qualify every lead on **Budget, Need, Authority, Timing** before you spend a sales call on them.

items: "this is four figures a month, any shock?"
"1–10, how bad? why not a 10? why not a 1?"
"if it fits, would you start this month?"

cards.plain: Most "bad leads" are unqualified leads. Four questions save hours and raise close rates.
cards.analogy: Ask whether the kid wants to play before selling the parents a 20-lesson pack.
cards.ex: Dental implants caller: Meta leads weren't the issue; the set call never asked budget or timing.
cards.move: Before booking a Day-1 trial: "How many caregivers do you hire in a normal month?" (need) + "are you the one who decides?" (authority) + timing.
cards.trap: Asking BANT like an interrogation. Ask it as a conversation.
cards.memo: **"Can pay, needs it, can decide, now."**
q: What do the 1–10 follow-ups do?
"Why not 10?" reveals doubts; "why not 1?" makes them sell themselves.

cards.hook: Short answers hide the real pain. **"Tell me more. Give me an example. What did that cost you?"**

vis.title: Dig until the pain is specific

cards.plain: People buy to fix specific, felt problems. Keep asking for examples and consequences until they say the cost out loud. Their words become your pitch.
cards.analogy: "My backhand is bad" → "show me" → "it's the late contact on high balls". Now you can fix it.
cards.ex: His live: alternate "can you give me an example?" and "can you be more specific?" when you get one-word answers.
cards.move: On every call get one number: shifts uncovered last week, hours they spent screening, a client lost. Write it down.
cards.trap: Accepting "it's fine" and moving to the pitch.
q: Two pull-teeth questions?
"Can you give me an example?" and "Can you be more specific?"

cards.hook: After an objection: **Acknowledge, Associate, Ask**. Then run a close. Repeat. The rep who asks most closes most.

vis.title: The loop
steps: "the best owners I work with said the same"
reason, hypothetical, zoom out, 1–10, best/worst case

cards.plain: Don't argue. Agree with the feeling, show others felt it and still won, then ask a question that makes them resolve it. Five universal closes rotate.
cards.analogy: Rally, don't smash every ball: keep it in play until the opening appears.
cards.ex: Course: only questions, no statements; ask more times rather than arguing.
cards.move: Write your 5 closes for the trial: hypothetical ("if a caregiver started Monday, what changes?"), zoom out ("in 6 months, what if nothing changes?"), 1–10, best/worst case, reason.
cards.trap: Arguing with facts. Facts rarely change feelings.
q: AAA stands for?
Acknowledge, Associate, Ask.

cards.hook: Every objection is one of five: **time, money, decision-maker, fit, stall**. Each has a reframe.

items: time = priorities; what's it costing you now?
"what if they say no?" support, not permission

cards.plain: "Let me think about it" means a fear wasn't addressed. Find which of the five it is and use that reframe with AAA.
cards.analogy: A kid "doesn't want to play" usually means "scared of losing". Fix the real one.
cards.ex: "Let me think about it" → "totally, what part are you thinking about?" (his live).
cards.move: Most likely for owners: money ("we use Indeed") → compare to the recruiter cost of $4,800–8,000/hire; stall → First Hire Free removes risk.
cards.trap: Treating the stated objection as the real one.
q: What's behind "let me think about it"?
An unaddressed fear; ask what part they're thinking about.

cards.hook: Same script, different results: **loud enough, slow enough, certain**. Memorise the words so you can focus on how you say them.

items: downward tone at the end of statements

cards.plain: Write the script, memorise it (black out one word each pass), then mark pauses and pitch changes. When you don't think about words, you can listen.
cards.analogy: Footwork drills until automatic, so in a match you only think about the point.
cards.ex: Brutally honest live: "you're not making the money because you're saying the wrong words, the wrong way".
cards.move: Black-out drill on your opener this week: 10 reads, one word blacked each time. Record one run a day.
cards.trap: Rushing because you're nervous. Slow = confident.
q: How does black-out memorisation work?
Read aloud, black out one word, read again; repeat until you know it cold.
clip: Right words, right way: tone, pauses, memorising

cards.hook: Showing beats telling. **Proof > promise**, and demonstration is the most underused proof.
cards.plain: The same offer with real results outsells a better offer with none. Start free to get proof; then use the strongest kind you can.
cards.analogy: Hit the shot in front of them instead of explaining your forehand.
cards.ex: First live: effort-based proof when you have no results ("35,000 pieces"). Then 10 free clients → testimonials → next 10 paid.
cards.move: First trial agency = your case study: record numbers (shifts covered, days to first caregiver). Founding 5 = case study + 2 intros.
cards.trap: Waiting for "enough proof" before selling.
q: Strongest proof type?
Demonstration.

cards.hook: Hire reps who've sold **your prospect, your process, your product** (2 of 3 at least, prospect most).

items: sold to this kind of buyer (most important)
at least a year of experience

cards.plain: Prove the script yourself first; then hire several at once. If 2 of 5 succeed the process works; if all fail, it's you.
cards.analogy: Hire a coach who has taught kids before, not just a great player.
cards.ex: Course: group first calls, a 60-second selfie video, skills call = first coaching session.
cards.move: Not before you've closed agencies yourself with the script.
cards.trap: Hiring a rep to "figure out sales" for you.
q: Which P matters most?
Prospect.
clip: What to look for when hiring a salesperson

cards.hook: **Your worst rep is your real standard.** Train daily with role-play and one number.
cards.plain: 14-day bootcamp, 25 script reads a day, role-play every day, a daily huddle with one number, weekly 1:1 with one KPI and one behaviour. Praise specific behaviour publicly.
cards.analogy: Drills before matches: every day, same structure, one thing to fix.
cards.ex: Daily huddle number (sales live); cancer star: fire the top performer who poisons culture.
cards.move: Use the same loop on yourself: daily read, one recording, one behaviour to fix.
cards.trap: "Be more confident": not a behaviour. Make it observable.
q: What does your worst rep show?
The real standard you tolerate.

cards.hook: "Sounds good so far? … **It is expensive, it's $X.**" Then say nothing for 8+ seconds.
cards.plain: Naming it "expensive" disarms: broke buyers brace, rich buyers find it less than feared. The silence lets them decide; filling it lets them off the hook.
cards.analogy: After the serve toss, you don't stop to explain the swing.
cards.ex: Course: reps who wait 8+ seconds close ~30% more.
cards.move: Practise the line and count 8 seconds in your head on every pitch.
cards.trap: Justifying the price before they react.
q: How long do you stay silent?
8+ seconds.
clip: When they say yes: stop selling, close

cards.t: BAMFAM: book a meeting from a meeting
cards.hook: **Never end a call without the next one booked.** If no sale, book the follow-up before hanging up.
cards.plain: A follow-up with a time is 5× more likely to happen than "I'll call you". Shrink it until they say yes.
cards.analogy: Ending a lesson with "same time Thursday?" instead of "let me know".
cards.ex: Course: "when were you planning to let me know?" → make that the meeting.
cards.move: Every "not now" owner: book a callback in the dialer with a date, plus send the Hiring Snapshot.
cards.trap: "I'll send info and follow up."
q: Last-resort BAMFAM line?
"When were you planning to let me know?" then book that.
clip: BAMFAM: book a meeting from a meeting

cards.hook: Right after they buy: **"Who else do you know who's as awesome as you?"** then a live intro.
cards.plain: Buyers are happiest at the moment of purchase. Referrals close higher with no price resistance.
cards.analogy: The parent who just signed up brings a friend to the next class.
cards.ex: Course: half are asked on the call; buyers not asked go to the top of the follow-up list.
cards.move: Founding 5 includes 2 intros: ask on the yes and on the day-25 results call. Intros, not paid referrals (legal line).
cards.trap: Waiting months to ask.
q: When to ask?
Immediately after the yes, and after the first win.
clip: Fastest leads: who has your customers first
cards.clipNote: Alex Hormozi in the course lesson closest to this idea ("Lead getters: referrals, affiliates, agencies, employees").

cards.hook: Send a short video **before every call** so prospects arrive pre-sold: the rep just makes a "six-inch putt".
cards.plain: A VSL answers the FAQs and builds belief before the call. It's mostly "proof salad". Mine sales calls for "why people buy" and put those words in the VSL.
cards.analogy: Kids who watched a 2-minute video of the drill learn it in half the time on court.
cards.ex: ACQ took only the pain points buyers said on calls, put them in the VSL, and acquisition roughly doubled.
cards.move: Record a 3-minute phone video for owners: promise, pain (no-shows), proof, plan (trial), CTA. Send it after booking.
cards.trap: Polished, generic VSLs with no proof.
q: What's "proof salad"?
