Proof shown many ways so viewers see themselves in it.
clip: Mine calls for "why people buy" → VSL

cards.hook: Measure **every step**: dials → connects → conversations → sets → shows → closes. The worst ratio is your next fix.
cards.plain: "Sales are bad" is useless. Ratios tell you which step to fix: script, list, targeting, follow-up or offer.
cards.analogy: Stats per match: first-serve %, unforced errors. You fix the worst one.
cards.ex: Course gates: cap at 3 sets/day until show rate >60% (target 70–75%).
cards.move: Log each step in the dialer. After 2 weeks, find your worst ratio and fix only that.
cards.trap: Only tracking closes.
q: Target show rate?
Above 60%, ideally 70–75%.

cards.hook: **Money objections are value objections.** Offer a real Ferrari for $5k and they'd find the money.

vis.title: The gap
vis.note: If value ÷ price feels big enough, money appears. Raise the value they see; don't cut the price.

cards.plain: Ask what it would cost them to keep the problem. Compare to the right alternative. Resourcefulness: people find money for what they truly value.
cards.analogy: Parents "can't afford" lessons but buy a €200 racket when the kid starts winning.
cards.ex: Course: the Ferrari test; time = priorities, money = value.
cards.move: "What does one uncovered shift cost you?" Then the recruiter anchor. Then First Hire Free removes the risk entirely.
cards.trap: Dropping the price at the first "too expensive".
q: What's the Ferrari test?
If the value were obvious (a real Ferrari for $5k), they'd find the money.

cards.hook: "Not now" usually means fear. Show **what waiting costs**, and that direction beats perfect timing.
cards.plain: Quantify the cost of inaction in their numbers. Point out they've tried waiting before ("burned twice"). Direction, not perfection.
cards.analogy: Waiting for "the right moment" to fix a hitch in your serve; it only gets grooved deeper.
cards.ex: Course: stall → quantify the cost of inaction; "let me think about it" → "what part are you thinking about?"
cards.move: "If nothing changes for 3 months, how many shifts go uncovered?" Then: the trial costs nothing to start.
cards.trap: Accepting "call me in a few months" without a booked time (BAMFAM).
q: Response to a stall?
Quantify the cost of inaction, then book the next step.

cards.hook: Wealth is a **sequence**, not a pile of tips: Margin → Optionality → $100k → Equity rich → Your terms.

vis.title: Each milestone unlocks the next
vis.note: You are on M. Skipping steps (investing before a margin) is how people stay broke with nice spreadsheets.

cards.plain: Most advice is random ("max your 401k", "buy ETFs"). The Wealth Roadmap gives an order: first stop falling behind, then build a cushion, then let money compound, then own assets, then live on what they pay.
cards.analogy: You don't enter tournaments before you can rally. Margin is the rally.
cards.ex: Course: business owners pour everything back into the business and never build personal wealth because nobody gave them a sequence.
cards.move: Your milestone is **M**: 90 days where tennis + agency income > your monthly costs. Track it in Money → Wealth. Frugal "needs only" is already the right play.
cards.trap: Investing or buying "assets" before you have margin.
cards.memo: **M-O-N-E-Y: Make more than you spend, Own time, Net 100k, Equity, Your terms.**
q: What's milestone O?
Optionality: 6–12 months of essential expenses in a separate account.
What unlocks $100k?
Having margin and a cushion first, so money can be invested and left alone.

cards.hook: Margin = **income bigger than expenses, every month, for 90 days**. Without it, nothing else works.
cards.plain: Know your monthly nut (what life costs), split essentials from extras, and make income exceed it consistently. Raise income first; cut only what you don't value.
cards.analogy: Winning more points than you lose each game. Do it consistently and the set takes care of itself.
cards.ex: Course: write your monthly nut; the goal is 90 straight days of positive margin.
cards.move: Your War Room Money tab already computes the nut. Next lever is income (first agency), not cutting more.
cards.trap: Cutting coffee while ignoring the big income lever.
q: How long must margin hold?
90 days.

cards.hook: Save **6–12 months of essentials** in a separate account so a bad month never forces a bad decision.
cards.plain: This is not investing money; it's time. If income stops, you have months to rebuild instead of taking the first bad deal.
cards.analogy: A spare racket in the bag: when a string breaks you keep playing.
cards.ex: War Room Wealth tab: target = essentials × 6, held in a separate savings account.
cards.move: After margin: send a fixed % of each payment to a separate account the day it lands.
cards.trap: Keeping it in the same account you spend from.
cards.memo: **"Months of runway = freedom to say no."**
q: Where should it live?
A separate account, not your spending account.

cards.hook: At ~$100k invested, **your money starts earning meaningful money while you sleep**. Freeze lifestyle to get there.

vis.title: Same 8%/yr return, different base
vis.note: Illustrative only, not advice: the point is that returns scale with the base.

cards.plain: Net financial assets = cash and investments minus consumer debt (not your home). Freeze lifestyle when income rises, send the difference to the "money factory", and review a monthly net-worth statement.
cards.analogy: Once your kids' group is big enough, the older kids help the younger ones: the group starts teaching itself.
cards.ex: Course: freeze lifestyle, money factory, monthly net-worth statement (War Room writes it automatically).
cards.move: Later. For now the factory is your earning power: the agency.
cards.trap: Lifestyle rising with every raise.
q: What's excluded from net financial assets?
Your home; card debt is subtracted.

cards.hook: Four monsters eat wealth silently: **inflation, taxes, interruption, fees**.

items: separate tax preparer vs tax strategist
emergencies, health, bad decisions: written rules

cards.plain: You can do everything right and still lose to these. Defend against each: invest beyond cash, plan taxes, keep written rules, minimise fees.
cards.analogy: Unforced errors: no opponent needed, they still cost you the match.
cards.ex: Course: separate preparer (files) from strategist (plans).
cards.move: Educational only, not advice. For you now: pay taxes on time, keep a written money rule list.
cards.trap: Ignoring 1–2% fees because they look small.
q: The four money monsters?
Inflation, taxes, interruption, fees.
clip: Sharran: taxes and fees drag wealth

cards.hook: **Equity rich**: $1M net worth without your home. **Your terms**: assets pay your life.
cards.plain: Equity rich usually comes from owning things that grow (a business, real estate, investments). Your terms means passive income covers expenses, so work becomes optional.
cards.analogy: The club owner who no longer needs to coach every session to pay the bills.
cards.ex: Course: $1M ex-home ≈ US accredited investor; coverage ratio = passive income ÷ expenses.
cards.move: Your fastest equity is a business that runs without you (see Scaling). Long game.
cards.trap: Confusing a high income with being equity rich.
q: Your-terms test?
Passive income ÷ expenses ≥ 100%.

cards.hook: You're not calling to convince. You're calling to **find out if there's a problem**. Yes and no are both fine answers.

b: they relax and tell the truth

cards.plain: Set your intent before every dial: you hold a guess that they might have a problem, not an assumption that they need you. Letting go of the outcome removes the neediness buyers sense.
cards.analogy: A coach doing a free trial session: "let's see if this is a fit for your kid" sells more than "sign up today".
cards.ex: Braun's cure for call reluctance: the anxiety comes from needing a yes; drop the need and the dread drops with it.
cards.move: Before each block, say it: "I'm sorting owners into has-a-hiring-problem / doesn't." A "no" is a sorted card, not a failure.
cards.trap: Fake detachment while still pushing for the meeting.
q: What's your intent on a cold call?
Find the truth: is there a problem worth talking about? Both answers are fine.
clip: The cure for cold calling reluctance
Why cold calling gives you anxiety

cards.hook: "Hi, it's Egor. **We've never spoken.** You weren't expecting my call. Could you help me out for a brief moment?" Then pause.
cards.plain: Honesty lowers the shield. Asking for help hands them control; once they say yes, they tend to listen (consistency). Rotate openers and keep what fits your voice.
cards.analogy: Knocking politely vs barging into someone's practice court.
cards.ex: Braun's first-30-seconds videos: no "how are you", no "reason for my call", no "27 seconds".
cards.move: Test this opener against your current one for 50 dials each; keep the one with more owner talks.
cards.trap: Saying it fast and chirpy. The words only work with a calm tone.
cards.memo: **"Name, never spoken, not expecting, help me?"**
q: Why ask for help?
It gives them control and triggers consistency once they say yes.
clip: The first 5 seconds of a cold call

cards.hook: Ask how they do it now as **multiple choice**: A and B are the usual ways, C is the better way you enable.

items: "…or keep a bench of pre-screened caregivers?"

cards.plain: Everyone already does the job somehow. Multiple choice is easy to answer, proves you're an insider, and often triggers "what's C?"
cards.analogy: "Do you practise serves alone, with a coach, or with a ball machine and video?"
cards.ex: Part of Braun's 4-step call: opener → right person → ABC → "you've probably considered" question.
cards.move: "When a caregiver quits, do you post on Indeed, call a staffing agency, or pull from a bench you already have?"
cards.trap: Making C sound like a pitch.
q: What does C do?
Names the better way you enable, so they ask about it.

cards.hook: Don't pitch. Ask a **neutral question that exposes a problem** they may not see, then go silent.

steps: "how do you handle X when Y happens?"

cards.plain: A problem they discover feels true; a problem you claim feels like a pitch. Make the question specific and neutral.
cards.analogy: "How's your second serve holding up in tight sets?" makes the player feel the problem.
cards.ex: Running-store gait test, Stripe failed-payment report: questions that reveal a hidden cost.
cards.move: "Not sure if this happens to you, but when a caregiver no-shows at 7 am, how do you cover the shift?"
cards.trap: Leading questions that obviously set up your product.
q: Why is a poke better than a claim?
People believe problems they discover themselves.

cards.hook: When they ask what you do: **"You know how [painful status quo]? We make that go away."** Then stop.
cards.plain: One sentence, the problem that differentiates you, no how-it-works. Pausing makes them ask for more.
cards.analogy: A one-line tip to a parent: "you know how kids lose interest when drills are boring? We make every drill a game."
cards.ex: Braun live critique: "what do you do?" answered in one line, then silence.
cards.move: "You know how owners lose clients when a caregiver doesn't show? I keep a bench ready so that shift gets covered."
cards.trap: Explaining the process.
cards.memo: **"You know how… we make it go away."**
q: What do you leave out?
How it works, features, category labels.
clip: Live cold call critique: what do you do?

cards.hook: It's the truth, not an objection. **Pause, "that's okay"**, compliment the tool, ask about its known weak spot.
cards.plain: Fighting the vendor makes them defend their choice. Agree, then explore the gap.
cards.analogy: "You have a coach? Great. How's it going on match days when he's not there?"
cards.ex: Braun: name the likely vendors up front (ABC) to pre-empt it.
cards.move: "That's okay, most owners use Indeed or an agency. How fast do they replace a caregiver who quits in week one?"
cards.trap: "But we're different!"
q: First response?
Pause, "that's okay", then curiosity about the gap.
clip: Defusing "we already work with a vendor"

cards.hook: React like a human, not a rep. **Lower the temperature**, don't push for 30 more seconds.

b: one soft question or let go

cards.plain: Early "not interested" is a reflex to the interruption. Acknowledge it, maybe ask one low-pressure question, and accept no gracefully.
cards.analogy: A kid says "I don't want to play" when cold; warm-up, not argument.
cards.ex: Braun's polls: most reps instinctively push. The friendly response gets more conversations.
cards.move: "Totally fair, I called out of nowhere. Mind if I ask one thing before I go?" If no: "No problem, have a good day."
cards.trap: Arguing with a reflex.
q: Why not push?
It raises resistance; most early no's are reflex to the interruption.
clip: A counterintuitive way to defuse objections

cards.hook: Delivery carries the message: **calm, slow, matter-of-fact**, like an equal over coffee.
cards.plain: Memorise the words, then record yourself and work on pace, pauses and pitch. Detachment makes the calm tone natural.
cards.analogy: The calm coach the kids listen to vs the shouting one they tune out.
cards.ex: Braun: late-night DJ voice; same as Voss's FM DJ voice.
cards.move: Record one call a day; listen only for pace and pitch at the end of sentences (down, not up).
cards.trap: Upward inflection on statements: sounds unsure.
q: What do you work on after memorising?
Pace, pauses and pitch.
clip: Cold calling that feels good on your soul

cards.hook: Early price questions are usually **curiosity, not buying**. Give a range honestly, then ask what they're comparing it to.
cards.plain: Dodging the price kills trust. A range plus a question keeps the conversation going and anchors.
cards.analogy: "Lessons are €20–40 depending on group size; what level is your kid?"
cards.ex: Braun: prospect asks "what's the price?"
cards.move: "Agencies pay from $1,500 a hire to $2,500 every 4 weeks for two working caregivers, depending on how many you hire monthly. How many is normal for you?"
cards.trap: "I'll get to that later."
q: Why not dodge?
It destroys trust; give a range and keep talking.

cards.hook: Lead with **one vivid problem peers complain about**, one plain sentence of solution, one easy ask.

steps: "owners tell me no-shows wreck their week"

cards.plain: Problem language converts about 2–3× better than buzzword value props. Use the words customers use.
cards.analogy: "Losing tight matches on double faults?" beats "holistic serve development".
cards.ex: 30MPC cold-call masterclass: the value-proposition script section.
cards.move: Pick the #1 problem you hear on calls and open every pitch with it, in their words.
cards.trap: Features and buzzwords.
q: Why problem first?
People react to pain they recognise; it converts 2–3× better.

cards.hook: Never "how's your day?". Open with **context about them**: a trigger or a common thread with customers.

b: "heard your name come up with other agency owners"

cards.plain: Context earns the next 10 seconds. Admit it's a cold call, ask for a moment, then deliver the problem. Tone beats exact words.
cards.analogy: "I watched your match Saturday" opens better than "hey, how are you".
cards.ex: "Triple your cold call meetings" script: the opener part.
cards.move: Use their Indeed job post as the trigger: "saw you've got a caregiver opening up on Indeed…"
cards.trap: Generic openers that sound like every other rep.
q: Best trigger for agencies?
A live caregiver job posting.

cards.hook: Early objections are reactions to the interruption: **agree, give a reason to keep talking, ask a choice question, sell the test drive**.

steps: small next step, not the car

cards.plain: Disarm, then incentivise one more answer. Sell a small next step (a short call, a trial), not the whole deal. Chain it for repeated objections.
cards.analogy: Wax on, wax off: deflect the strike, don't block it head-on.
cards.ex: 30MPC script: Mr. Miyagi section; "sell the test drive, not the car".
cards.move: "Makes sense, and so I don't call you again: is hiring more of a volume problem or a no-show problem?" Then: First Hire Free = the test drive.
cards.trap: Selling the full plan on a cold call.
q: What do you sell on a cold call?
The test drive (small next step), not the car.
clip: Sell the test drive, not the car

cards.hook: Treat the gatekeeper as **a person who can help**, not an obstacle. Be brief, specific and confident.
cards.plain: Confidence and specificity get you through; tricks get you blocked. Learn names and come back.
cards.analogy: The club receptionist decides who gets the good court times. Be nice to them.
cards.ex: 30MPC masterclass: getting past gatekeepers.
cards.move: "Hi, it's Egor. I'm calling about caregiver hiring; who usually handles that?"
cards.trap: Lying about who you are.
q: Best gatekeeper question?
"Who handles caregiver hiring?"

cards.hook: Leave **two short voicemails**: context, no pitch, no callback request, point to your email or text.
cards.plain: Voicemails lift reply rates on the other channel and make later pickups warmer. Never pitch on voicemail.
cards.analogy: A quick note in the parent's mailbox that points to the flyer.
cards.ex: 30MPC: calls and voicemails roughly double to triple email reply rates.
cards.move: No answer → 15-second voicemail + text with the Monday Bench Bulletin offer.
cards.trap: Long pitch voicemails asking for a callback.
cards.memo: **"Short, no pitch, point to the text."**
q: What should a voicemail do?
Point to your email/text; no pitch, no callback ask.

cards.t: Status tactics: pre-pitch pushaway & checking for agreement
cards.hook: Higher status = **you're evaluating them too**. Push away before you pitch; check agreement instead of assuming it.

items: "this might not be for you, but…"

cards.plain: Eager sellers sound low status. Showing you'll walk away makes buyers lean in.
cards.analogy: The club with a waiting list feels better than the one begging for members.
cards.ex: 30MPC: 9 psychological tactics to raise your status (chapters linked).
cards.move: Before pitching the trial: "Honestly, this only works for agencies hiring at least one caregiver a month. Is that you?"
cards.trap: Pushaway that sounds arrogant.
q: What does a pushaway do?
Shows you're evaluating fit too, which raises your status.

cards.hook: **10–15 touches over 3–4 weeks** across phone, voicemail, email/text and LinkedIn, all using one research hook.
cards.plain: Most meetings come after touch 4+. Cluster touches, vary channels, reuse one hook.
cards.analogy: A kid needs to hear "bend your knees" many times in different ways before it sticks.
cards.ex: 30MPC perfect outbound sequence.
cards.move: Every owner who doesn't answer enters a 3-week cadence in your dialer; stop only on a clear no.
cards.trap: One call, then giving up.
q: How many touches?
About 10–15 over 3–4 weeks.

cards.hook: End discovery with two questions: **"Is this worth solving?" … "Is it worth solving now?"** Silence after each.
cards.plain: Structure the call so the buyer decides if and when, then prescribe how they buy, including the step after next.
cards.analogy: "Do you want to fix your serve? Before the summer tournament?"
cards.ex: 30MPC: how to structure the perfect discovery call.
cards.move: After the hiring pain: "Is this worth fixing? … Before the next caregiver quits?" Then offer First Hire Free.
cards.trap: Assuming urgency they never said.
q: The two questions?
Is this worth solving? Is it worth solving now?
clip: The upfront agenda: purpose, questions, next step

cards.hook: Name the feeling: **"It sounds like…" / "It seems like…"**, no "I", then silence.

steps: "it sounds like you've been burned by agencies"

cards.plain: Labels make people feel understood and draw out more than direct questions. Leaving out "I" keeps it about them.
cards.analogy: "Looks like that loss is still bugging you" opens a player up more than "what's wrong?"
cards.ex: Voss calls labels his most versatile tool: every type of negotiator ranks them among what they most want used on them.
cards.move: When an owner sighs about hiring: "It sounds like you've tried a lot of things that didn't stick." Then shut up.
cards.trap: "I hear you saying…": puts you in the middle.
q: Why leave out "I"?
It keeps the focus on them and sounds observational, not personal.

cards.hook: Summarise their world until they say **"That's right."** "You're right" means "please stop talking".
cards.plain: A summary that includes their fears and even the bad things they think about you produces a small epiphany that bonds them to you.
cards.analogy: Repeating a kid's frustration back until they nod: now they'll listen to the fix.
cards.ex: Voss: what is better than "yes"? "That's right."
cards.move: Before pitching: "So you've got shifts uncovered most weeks, Indeed sends people who don't show, and you're doing interviews at night." Wait for "that's right".
cards.trap: Summaries that are really pitches.
q: What does "you're right" usually mean?
"Please stop talking."

cards.hook: Ask **"how" and "what"**, not "why". They make people think and give them the feeling of control.

b: "how would you like it to work?"

cards.plain: Open questions trigger slow thinking and point toward implementation. Use "why" only surgically.
cards.analogy: "What made that point hard?" vs "why did you miss that?"
cards.ex: Voss: how and when to use "why".
cards.move: Swap "why don't you…" for "what's stopped that from working so far?"
cards.trap: Rapid-fire questions without listening.
q: Why avoid "why"?
It makes people defensive.

cards.hook: Ask questions where **"no" is the yes**: "Is it a ridiculous idea to…?" "Are you against…?"
cards.plain: Saying no makes people feel safe and in control, so they relax and volunteer real obstacles. People are "yes-battered" by tie-down selling.
cards.analogy: "Would you hate it if we tried one new drill?" gets a happier "no".
cards.ex: Voss: using "no" to persuade people quickly.
cards.move: "Would it be a terrible idea to see who's on the bench this week?"
cards.trap: Stacking yes-questions ("right? right?").
q: Why does no feel safe?
It protects autonomy; they feel in control.

cards.hook: Say the negatives **before they do**: "You're probably thinking this is another agency pitch…"
cards.plain: Naming a negative shrinks it; denying it ("I don't want you to think…") plants and magnifies it.
cards.analogy: "This drill will feel boring at first" makes kids less likely to complain.
cards.ex: Voss: say it as an observation, never a denial.
cards.move: Opener add-on: "You probably get ten calls a week from staffing people, and most waste your time."
cards.trap: "I'm not trying to sell you anything": a denial.
q: Observation or denial?
Observation. Denial magnifies the negative.
clip: Be Nice -OR- BEWARE! | The Power of an Accusations Audit | Chris Voss
cards.clipBy: Chris Voss & The Black Swan Group

cards.hook: Repeat their **last 1–3 words** as a curious question. They expand, you learn more.
cards.plain: Mirrors work almost invisibly, buy you time and make people restate things in new words.
cards.analogy: Echoing a kid's "it's too hard?" so they explain which part.
cards.ex: Voss toolkit, used heavily by Braun too.
cards.move: Use one mirror per call when an owner says something vague.
cards.trap: Mirroring everything like a parrot.
q: How many words?
One to three, usually the last ones.
clip: Talk Like a Pro: Master Labels, Mirrors & Questions to Win Any Conversation!
cards.clipBy: Chris Voss & The Black Swan Group

cards.hook: Your voice changes their brain before your words land. **Calm, slow, downward** = late-night FM DJ.

items: speeds people up, makes them like you (default)

cards.plain: Default to playful; use the DJ voice for important points and to calm tension; avoid assertive.
cards.analogy: Same words from a calm vs shouting coach land completely differently.
cards.ex: Voss: three voices.
cards.move: Price and guarantee lines in DJ voice; opener in a smiling, playful voice.
cards.trap: Assertive voice when nervous.
cards.memo: **"Smile mostly, DJ for the big lines."**
q: Which voice to avoid?
Assertive.
clip: Make Them Listen: How To Use Your Tone To Control Their Reactions
cards.clipBy: Chris Voss & The Black Swan Group

cards.hook: People love correcting you. Lay out your **best guess**; a correction tells you the real story.

steps: "sounds like the issue is pay rates"

cards.plain: Whether you hear "that's right" or a correction, you're collaborating and learning the truth.
cards.analogy: "So you mostly lose on your backhand?" "No, it's my footwork." Now you know.
cards.ex: Voss: get the truth without asking for it directly.
cards.move: "I'd guess your biggest problem is finding people at all?" Let them correct you.
cards.trap: Insulting guesses.
q: Why guess wrong on purpose?
People correct instinctively and reveal the real situation.
clip: Get the truth without asking for it

cards.hook: Under pressure **you fall to your level of preparation**. ~60 correct reps make a skill automatic.

vis.title: Reps until it feels natural (his estimate)

cards.plain: New skills feel awkward because a new pathway is forming. Most quit just before the breakthrough. Practise in low-stakes moments.
cards.analogy: A new grip feels wrong for weeks, then it's yours.
cards.ex: Voss: a 15-minute daily habit.
cards.move: Use one Voss tool on purpose every day (labels in tennis lessons count).
cards.trap: Trying a new tool once on a big call and dropping it.
q: Where do you practise?
Low-stakes moments, every day.

cards.hook: Agencies don't have a hiring problem. They have **five systems** that leak: culture, recruiting, selection, onboarding, retention.
cards.plain: Tweed treats caregiver staffing as five linked systems. A leak anywhere empties the bucket, so fixing recruiting alone rarely fixes "we can't staff cases".
cards.analogy: A tennis club that signs up new kids but loses them after 3 lessons doesn't need more ads; it needs a better first month.
cards.ex: An owner says "we need more applicants". Ask where they lose people: before the interview, in week one, or at month three.
cards.move: On calls, place Caregiver Bench in his steps: you speed up recruiting and selection, and your 90-day Stay-or-Replace covers the onboarding window.
cards.trap: Pitching "more applicants" to an owner whose real leak is week-one no-shows.
q: Name the 5 systems.
Culture, recruiting, selection, onboarding, retention.

cards.hook: Most caregiver turnover happens in the **first 90 days**. That window is where an owner bleeds money.
cards.plain: The hardest part isn't hiring, it's keeping someone through the first three months. Rewarding staying (not just joining) and a strong first week cut the leak.
cards.analogy: New tennis kids: if they enjoy the first month, they stay for years.
cards.ex: Replacing a caregiver costs an agency roughly $2,500–5,000 (Library II data). A 90-day guarantee speaks straight to that cost.
cards.move: Lead with your 90-Day Stay-or-Replace when an owner mentions turnover. Ask: "How many of last quarter's hires are still with you?"
cards.trap: Celebrating a placement on day 1 and disappearing until there's a problem.
q: Why does the 90-day window matter for your offer?
Most turnover happens there, and replacing a caregiver costs the agency thousands.
clip: Home Care Stats You Need To Know: Retention - Part 3
cards.clipNote: The same skill taught by a different, credible teacher. No video of the original author was found.

cards.hook: Median caregiver turnover ~**75%** a year. Top agencies stay under 40%. Pay and **speed** make the gap.

vis.title: Annual turnover by pay band (2025 data)

cards.plain: The median agency loses about three quarters of its caregivers a year. Indeed is a top source, referrals second; about 800 applicants become ~63 hires. The best agencies interview within 24–48 hours.
cards.analogy: Like a bucket with a hole: pouring faster (more ads) helps less than patching the hole.
cards.ex: "Most agencies lose 3 of 4 caregivers a year. Where are you on that?" is a strong discovery question because the owner knows his number.
cards.move: Use one number per call, never a lecture: turnover, cost of a replacement, or speed to interview. Then ask about theirs.
cards.trap: Reciting statistics instead of asking about their own numbers.
q: What interview speed do the best agencies hit?
Within 24–48 hours of applying.
clip: Home Care Stats You Need To Know: Retention - Part 3

cards.t: Stay on the right side of Florida law
cards.hook: Nurse registries refer **contractors**. You recruit for **licensed agencies** that hire W-2. Different lane, different rules.
cards.plain: Florida treats referral businesses tightly (Patient Brokering Act; registry rules from 1 Jul 2026). Your safe lane: recruiting for licensed agencies, flat fees, the agency employs and places. Get the lawyer's written answer before the first invoice.
cards.analogy: Coaching a player vs entering the tournament for them: you prepare, the club fields the player.
cards.ex: If an owner offers to pay "per family you bring", the answer is no, every time.
cards.move: Keep the one-line legal frame ready: "We recruit and screen; you hire them as your W-2 employees. Flat fee, nothing per client."
cards.trap: Drifting into placing caregivers with families or charging per client to close a deal.
q: What makes a nurse registry different from you?
Registries refer independent contractors; you recruit for agencies that hire W-2.
cards.clipNote: Official AHCA video, but only on background screening (which agencies do, not us). No official video explains the licence types: read the three AHCA pages below.
cards.src: Florida AHCA: Nurse Registries; Homemaker and Companion Services FAQ; ss. 400.506 and 400.509 F.S. (read 19 Nov 2026)

cards.hook: If four recruiters chase the same order, each has a **25% commitment** and fills about 1 in 4. Ask for exclusivity.

a: you compete on speed and price

cards.plain: Savage: the intake call decides the fill. Never lie to candidates, fire clients who waste your time, and don't win on speed or price alone. Revenue over margin and ego kill recruiting firms.
cards.analogy: One coach per player. Three coaches giving one kid different advice gets nowhere.
cards.ex: An owner wants you "plus our other two agencies". Offer to take the hardest open case exclusively for 30 days instead.
cards.move: Make intake strict: exact shift, area, language, skills, pay, and "when can you interview?" before you source anyone.
cards.trap: Saying yes to every order and filling none of them well.
q: Why ask for exclusivity?
Multi-listed orders split commitment and get filled far less often.
clip: Recruitment Entrepreneurs Ep 20- Ft. Greg Savage | Recruit CRM
cards.clipNote: An interview or clip of the teacher, not from their own channel.

cards.hook: Early on, recruit customers **by hand** and serve them absurdly well. The manual work is what starts the compounding.
cards.plain: Graham's point: the first users don't come from a launch, they come from founders going out and getting them one by one, then over-serving them.
cards.analogy: Your first tennis students came from you asking parents directly, not from an ad.
cards.ex: First Hire Free on one open case, you personally screen every candidate and call the owner after each interview.
cards.move: Treat your first 3 agencies like VIPs: daily update, same-day replacements, a personal call at day 25.
cards.trap: Building automations and dashboards before anyone pays you.
q: What does "don't scale" look like for you this month?
Calling owners yourself and over-serving the first agencies personally.
clip: Paul Graham On Startups, Ambition, and Great Founders

cards.t: A few users who love you
cards.hook: **Fully satisfy a few** before partly satisfying many. It's easier to add users than to deepen love.
cards.plain: Deep satisfaction from a small group gives feedback, morale and word of mouth. Start narrow (one city, one niche) and win it before spreading.
cards.analogy: One club where every kid improves beats five clubs where nobody notices you.
cards.ex: Your Founding 5 agencies: price lock in exchange for a case study and 2 intros.
cards.move: Win Tampa Bay before adding Collier and Lee. Depth, then breadth.
cards.trap: Chasing more agencies while the first one is only "OK".
q: Why start narrow?
A few who love you give referrals and feedback; spreading thin gives neither.
clip: Mr. Startup: Paul Graham, founder of YCombinator, and his "no asshole" rule
cards.clipNote: An interview or clip of the teacher, not from their own channel.

cards.hook: Determination predicts founder success better than intelligence, but **relentlessly resourceful**, not rigid.

items: never stop heading for the goal
change the route on the fly

cards.plain: Like a running back: the goal stays fixed, the path changes. Half-hearted commitment is the most common way startups die, and they rarely die suddenly: founders fade.
cards.analogy: A match where plan A fails: you don't quit, you switch to plan B and keep competing.
cards.ex: No owner answers at 15:00 Moldova time? Change the hour, not the goal.
cards.move: When a block fails, change one variable (time, list, opener) and dial again the same day.
cards.trap: Calling stubbornness "determination" while repeating what doesn't work.
q: What kills most startups according to Graham?
Founders getting demoralized and fading; half-hearted commitment.
clip: Paul Graham - The Anatomy of Determination
cards.clipNote: An interview or clip of the teacher, not from their own channel.

cards.hook: Don't tell them they have a problem. **Ask questions until they tell you**, and what they say, they believe.
cards.plain: Miner's sequence moves from connection to situation, problem awareness, solution awareness and consequence before any presentation. Tone: curious, a little skeptical, concerned.
cards.analogy: A good coach asks "what happened on that point?" so the player sees the mistake himself.
cards.ex: "How do you handle it now when a caregiver no-shows?" → "What does that do to the family?" → "What does that cost you?"
cards.move: Combine: Braun opener → Miner middle (situation → problem → consequence) → Voss for price.
cards.trap: Rushing to the presentation after one problem question.
q: Which comes first: consequence or presentation?
Consequence. Present only after they feel what the problem costs.
clip: The Top 6 Sales Questions That Make Prospects Sell Themselves

cards.hook: Everything in your world is on you. **"My fault, here's my fix."** Ownership is the only path that gives you control.
cards.plain: Jocko: when things fail, own it and fix it, instead of blaming people, the market or bad luck. Owning doesn't make the problem vanish; it obliges you to solve it.
cards.analogy: Losing a match "because of the wind" teaches nothing. "I didn't adjust to the wind" gives you something to train.
cards.ex: "3 dials in 10 days" is not the calendar's fault. "I didn't start the block. Fix: first dial inside 2 minutes."
cards.move: In tonight's shutdown, write one failure of the day as "My fault: … My fix: …".
cards.trap: Ownership as self-attack. It's a fix, not a punishment.
q: What does ownership oblige you to do?
Fix the problem, not just admit it.

cards.hook: Discipline has to come **from inside**. Doing the necessary work is what frees you.
cards.plain: Get up, train, eat right, do tomorrow's list. Nobody supplies discipline for you; it's generated within. The freedom comes after the work, not instead of it.
cards.analogy: The player who did the boring drills is the one who's free to play creatively in the match.
cards.ex: Doing the 10 dials at 20:30 is what makes 20:45 shutdown and 21:00 sleep guilt-free.
cards.move: Pick the one discipline that frees the rest: the dial block starts on time. Everything else follows.
cards.trap: Waiting to "feel disciplined" before acting.
q: Where does discipline come from?
From within. Nobody can supply it for you.
clip: What Discipline Really Means - Jocko Willink

cards.hook: 100 priorities means none. Pick **the one or two that matter** and execute. In chaos: the next practical task.
cards.plain: When overwhelmed, step back, pick the highest-priority problem, attack it, then the next. Don't try to solve everything at once.
cards.analogy: Down 0–4: play the next point, not the whole set.
cards.ex: Instead of shipping app version 11, the one priority is starting the dial block.
cards.move: Every morning, write the one task that moves 1 July most. Do it before anything else work-related.
cards.trap: Calling a long to-do list "prioritised".
q: What do you focus on in chaos?
The next practical task on the top priority.
clip: How To Prioritize and Execute Tasks That Pile Up - Jocko Willink

cards.hook: Rehearse until it runs **without thought**. Under stress you don't rise, you fall back on your drills.

vis.title: Under pressure you do what you drilled

cards.plain: Huge repetition creates huge skill gaps. SEAL reload races, tripwire drills: the procedure is automatic, so the mind is free for the situation.
cards.analogy: Your serve toss under match pressure is only as good as the 10,000 tosses in practice.
cards.ex: "Too expensive" should trigger your Ferrari line without thinking, because you said it 50 times out loud.
cards.move: Pick the 3 objections you fear most. Say each answer 25× out loud this week (Friday hot-topic drill).
cards.trap: Rereading scripts instead of saying them out loud.
q: Why drill objection answers out loud?
Under stress you fall back on what you rehearsed, not what you read.
clip: Jocko on Training Hard and Getting Adequate Rest - Jocko Willink

cards.hook: After every block: **what worked, what didn't, what changes.** Write it down so the lesson survives.
cards.plain: Lessons that aren't captured get lost. Jocko's teams debriefed every operation and turned lessons into SOPs.
cards.analogy: Watching your match video with your coach the same evening.
cards.ex: Shutdown daily log: "Biggest mistake → what I do differently tomorrow (one tweak)".
cards.move: Every dial block ends with a 2-line debrief in War Room. One change only.
cards.trap: Debriefs that list 10 changes and change nothing.
q: What are the 3 debrief questions?
What worked, what didn't, what changes.
clip: Jocko Podcast 41 with Tony Eafrati - BTF BTF BTF BTF

cards.hook: Confidence is the **product** of doing hard things, not the entry ticket. You will never feel ready the first time.
cards.plain: Action creates experience, experience builds competence, competence produces confidence. Waiting to feel confident is waiting forever.
cards.analogy: Nobody feels confident at their first tournament. They feel it at their tenth.
cards.ex: Not "I'll call when I'm ready", but "I'll be ready after 100 calls".
cards.move: Your first 10 calls each block are reps, not tests. Ugly is allowed.
cards.trap: More preparation, more scripts, more app versions as a substitute for the first dial.
q: What comes first, confidence or action?
Action. Confidence is its product.
clip: Give me 15 Minutes and I'll Make you Dangerously Confident

cards.hook: Track **controllable inputs** daily, not moods. Look at the numbers even when you don't want to.
cards.plain: What gets measured improves; records beat the brain's emotional story. Leading indicators (dials, conversations) over lagging ones (revenue).
cards.analogy: The scale and the match stats don't care how hard you felt you trained.
cards.ex: War Room's dial counter is the truth-teller. Building tools isn't on it.
cards.move: Read your weekly dial number out loud at Sunday review before anything else.
cards.trap: Tracking outcomes you don't control and ignoring the inputs you do.
q: Inputs or outcomes?
Track controllable inputs daily: dials and conversations.
clip: Give me 26 minutes, and I'll Make You A Dangerous Entrepreneur

cards.hook: Willpower drains. Disciplined people **engineer their environment** so the right thing is the easy thing.
cards.plain: Remove friction from good habits, add it to bad ones, pre-decide alternatives, and replace habits rather than just removing them.
cards.analogy: Packing your tennis bag the night before so the 05:30 session needs zero decisions.
cards.ex: Phone charges outside the bedroom; the Dial screen opens first; the first number is pre-loaded.
cards.move: Before tonight's block: phone on Dial, laptop closed except War Room, first number ready.
cards.trap: Relying on "being motivated tonight".
q: What beats willpower?
Designing the environment so the right action is the easy one.
clip: Become Addicted To Discipline With These 6 Strategies

cards.t: Never decide in an emotional state
cards.hook: Strong emotion distorts judgment **like alcohol**. Big decisions only when calm; wait 24–48 hours.
cards.plain: Felt urgency is usually an illusion. Refuse pressure to rush deals or purchases; decide when you're calm and content.
cards.analogy: Never change your racket or grip in the middle of a tilted match.
cards.ex: The urge to pivot to HVAC after a bad week is an emotion. The 8 Dec review is the calm decision point.
cards.move: Write any "change everything" idea in the Sunday-review list instead of acting on it today.
cards.trap: Calling an emotional decision "being decisive".
q: How long should you wait on a big emotional decision?
24–48 hours, then decide when calm.
clip: opening up about my hardest moments

cards.hook: Know your hourly value and **offload everything worth less**. Time doesn't multiply; money does.

vis.title: Where an owner's hour should go

cards.plain: The first hire is usually an assistant. Spend money to free your attention for revenue-generating work.
cards.analogy: A pro player doesn't string his own rackets.
cards.ex: Later: a part-time screener takes caregiver phone screens so you stay on owner calls.
cards.move: Now: list your weekly tasks and mark which one you'd hand off first once money comes in.
cards.trap: Hiring before there's revenue, or doing $5 tasks forever after there is.
cards.memo: **"Buy back the hours that make money."**
q: What's usually the first hire?
An assistant to take low-value tasks off the owner.
clip: You're Procrastinating 80% of Your Time (Here's How I Fixed It)

cards.hook: People can't hit a standard they don't know or a number nobody measures.

vis.title: Accountability
top: who owns what, by when, how good
vis.note: Clear + measured + fast feedback. Teach through consequences, not lectures.

cards.plain: Define what each person owns, by when and to what standard; measure it; give feedback on the gap. No yelling, no lectures.
cards.analogy: "Practise more" changes nothing. "50 serves at 70% in, checked Friday" does.
cards.ex: Your own accountability: 350 dials a week, measured daily, reviewed Sunday.
cards.move: Apply it to yourself first: your weekly target, your measure, your Sunday feedback.
cards.trap: Expectations in your head that you never said out loud.
cards.memo: **"Expect it, measure it, feed it back."**
q: What three parts make accountability?
Expectations, measurement, feedback.
clip: If Your Team isn't Performing, Watch This

cards.hook: Hand off **thinking**, not just tasks. Stay nose in, hands off.
cards.plain: Delegate by importance and the person's skill. Each task gets a zone, so people know how much freedom they have.
cards.analogy: Assistant coach runs warm-ups alone (zone 1) but you decide match lineups (zone 4).
cards.ex: Future screener: phone screens zone 3, sending profiles to owners zone 2, pricing zone 4.
cards.move: When you hire, write the zone next to every task on the job description.
cards.trap: Delegating a task and then doing it yourself because "it's faster".
q: Name the four zones.
Done or deleted, informed of progress, informed of results, don't delegate.
clip: How To Do More In 4 WEEKS Than Most People Do In 4 Years

cards.hook: You fall to the level of your systems. A system without a **trigger, steps and tracking** isn't a system.
cards.plain: Vague systems can't repeat or scale. Audit and upgrade one piece at a time.
cards.analogy: Warm-up routine: trigger (arrive at court), steps (5 drills), tracked (done/not).
cards.ex: New applicant system: trigger = form submitted → call within 24h → screen script → mark in Bench.
cards.move: Write your applicant-to-screen system with all three parts this week.
cards.trap: "I'll just remember to do it."
q: What does every system need?
A trigger, exact steps and tracking.
clip: Success Is Hard Until You Build Systems Like This

cards.hook: Every emotion runs on **physiology, focus and language**. Change one and your state changes.

items: the words and meaning you use
vis.note: State drives behaviour. Fix the state before the dial block.

cards.plain: You can't think your way out of a low state while slumped on a chair. Move the body, change the focus, change the words.
cards.analogy: Bouncing on your toes and saying "come on" between points isn't decoration; it changes the next point.
cards.ex: War Room's 45-second Launch: stand, 3 breaths out loud, "my job is the dial, not the yes".
cards.move: Before every block: stand up, breathe, say your line. Then dial within 2 minutes.
cards.trap: Waiting for the right mood to start.
q: What three things drive state?
Physiology, focus, language.
clip: How to IMMEDIATELY Change Your Mental State - Tony Robbins Motivation
cards.clipNote: An interview or clip of the teacher, not from their own channel.

cards.hook: Every moment you decide **what to focus on, what it means, and what to do**.
cards.plain: Meaning creates emotion, emotion drives action. Change the meaning you give an event and the action changes.
cards.analogy: A double fault means either "I choke" or "adjust the toss". Same event, different match.
cards.ex: Rejection meaning "a no sorted, 9 more to a conversation" keeps you dialing.
cards.move: After each rude hang-up, say the meaning out loud: "Sorted. Next."
cards.trap: Letting the first meaning your brain offers decide the night.
q: Which of the three decisions creates emotion?
Meaning.
clip: 3 Decisions You Make Daily That Control & Shape Your Life

cards.hook: We always get our **musts**, rarely our shoulds. Raise the standard and you find a way.
cards.plain: Top performers share a hunger that doesn't fade. Standards, not goals, decide behaviour on bad days.
cards.analogy: You never "should" go to your own paid training. You just go.
cards.ex: Your minimum day: 10 dials + 25 min BAC, never 0. That's a must.
cards.move: Say your one must for tomorrow out loud tonight.
cards.trap: Ten musts. Then none of them are.
q: What do we always get?
Our musts.
clip: How To Raise Your Standards To Get ANYTHING YOU WANT

cards.hook: Not a to-do list: **what result, why it matters, and the massive action plan.**
cards.plain: Know the outcome and the reason before the tasks. Tell the truth about the gap, model the best, act imperfectly, measure, celebrate.
cards.analogy: "Win the regional" (R), "to get to the national team" (P), then the training plan (M).
cards.ex: R: first paying agency. P: freedom and proof. M: 350 dials a week, First Hire Free offer, follow-ups.
cards.move: Write a one-line RPM for this week at Sunday review.
cards.trap: A to-do list with no result and no reason.
q: What does RPM stand for?
Result, Purpose, Massive action plan.

cards.t: Follow up until they buy or die
cards.hook: The ad only **starts** the sale. The money is in organized, multi-step follow-up.
cards.plain: Intense short sequences, then steady maintenance contact. Unconverted leads can be worth as much as your current customers.
cards.analogy: Parents who say "maybe next season" sign up when you check in before the season starts.
cards.ex: Every "not now" gets the Monday Bench Bulletin and a recall date.
cards.move: No lead ever leaves the pipeline without a next touch date.
cards.trap: One call, one email, then forgetting them.
cards.memo: **"Follow up till they buy or die."**
q: Where is most of the money?
In the follow-up, not the first contact.
clip: How to Deal with the Endless Options in Marketing with Dan Kennedy

cards.t: Why you over everything, including doing nothing
cards.hook: Answer daily: **why should an owner choose you over every option, including doing nothing?**
cards.plain: A USP is a specific promise competitors can't easily copy, like Domino's 30-minute guarantee, not a slogan. Reinvent it when copied.
cards.analogy: "Lessons in Chisinau" vs "your kid serves overhand in 6 weeks or the next month is free".
cards.ex: Show-Up Guarantee (replacement in 24h) + 90-Day Stay-or-Replace is your teeth.
cards.move: Write your one-sentence answer to "why you over doing nothing" and use it on every call.
cards.trap: "Quality caregivers, great service." Everyone says that.
cards.memo: **"Why you, why now, why not nothing?"**
q: Who is your biggest competitor?
Doing nothing.
clip: Why You Should Make EVERYTHING An Opportunity Masterclass with Dan Kennedy

cards.hook: Start with **who**, go where the money is, and say what that market already worries about.

items: who exactly: Tampa Bay private-pay agency owners
their live worry: open cases, no-shows
how you reach them: the phone, then email

cards.plain: Without message-to-market match you arrive as an annoying pest instead of a welcome guest.
cards.analogy: Talking about topspin technique to a parent who only wants their kid to have fun.
cards.ex: Owners lie awake about unstaffed cases, not about "recruiting solutions".
cards.move: Open every call with their worry in their words: open cases, no-shows, turnover.
cards.trap: Picking the media first (ads, LinkedIn) before knowing the who.
q: What comes first: market, message or media?
Market.
clip: The Ultimate Lead Generation Machine with Dan Kennedy & Dave Dee (4 of 4) | Magnetic Marke

cards.t: One is the most dangerous number
cards.hook: One lead source, one platform, one client: **one is a single point of failure.**
cards.plain: Relying on one medium invites disaster. Combine channels once the first one works.
cards.analogy: A player with only a forehand gets broken the moment the opponent finds it.
cards.ex: Now: the phone. Next, once it works: email follow-ups, referrals, the Bench Bulletin.
cards.move: Phone first (Core Four focus), but plan the second channel for after 3 paying agencies.
cards.trap: Starting five channels at once to "diversify" before one works.
q: Why is one dangerous?
A single source can stop overnight.
clip: Internet Marketing Principles by Dan Kennedy | Magnetic Marketing

cards.hook: The **height of the step** you ask for decides how many take it.
cards.plain: Prospects are less ready and more intimidated than you think. Offer an easy first step beside the bigger ask.
cards.analogy: "Come watch one group session" beats "sign up for the year".
cards.ex: "Not now" owners: "Can I send you Monday's Bench Bulletin? Free, one email a week."
cards.move: Always have a smaller yes ready when the big ask gets a no.
cards.trap: Only offering the big commitment, then losing everyone who isn't ready today.
q: What's your low-threshold offer for a "not now"?
The free Monday Bench Bulletin (or Hiring Snapshot).
clip: How to Deal with the Endless Options in Marketing with Dan Kennedy

cards.hook: Partner with people **who already hold your buyers' trust** instead of only cold outreach.
cards.plain: Endorsed mailings, joint ventures and partner newsletters shortcut trust-building.
cards.analogy: The club owner recommending you to parents beats any flyer.
cards.ex: Later: home care associations, staffing software vendors, agency consultants.
cards.move: List 3 people or groups Tampa owners already trust. Don't contact yet: calls first.
cards.trap: Paying for referrals per client (illegal for you). Partnerships must stay flat-fee and legal.
cards.memo: **"Borrow trust, don't build it from zero."**
q: What makes a partner intro better than a cold call?
The partner already has the buyer's trust.
clip: Choreographing Your Sales Process Masterclass with Dan Kennedy

cards.hook: Ask **what would guarantee failure**, then avoid it fanatically.

steps: how would I make sure it never happens?
don't dial, change offer weekly, lie, ignore follow-ups

cards.plain: Berkshire won by being consistently not stupid rather than brilliant. Give dangers a wide berth and never risk ruin.
cards.analogy: Before a big match: "how would I lose this for sure?" Double-faulting, no warm-up, panicking. Fix those.
cards.ex: The fastest way to kill Caregiver Bench: no dials, constant pivots, a legal shortcut. Avoid those three and you're ahead of most.
cards.move: Write 5 ways to guarantee failure by 1 July. Read them on Sunday.
cards.trap: Only thinking about what to add, never what to stop.
cards.memo: **"Tell me where I'll die, so I never go there."**
q: What is inversion?
Solve a problem backwards: find what would cause failure and avoid it.
cards.clipBy: Seeking Wisdom: Value Investing & Worldly Wisdom
cards.clipNote: An interview or clip of the teacher, not from their own channel.

cards.hook: Never underestimate incentives. **People sincerely believe what pays them.**
cards.plain: Design systems so good behaviour pays, and distrust advice from people paid by the outcome.
cards.analogy: A coach paid per lesson has a reason to keep you needing lessons.
cards.ex: Your 90-Day Stay-or-Replace aligns your incentive with the owner's: you win when caregivers stay.
cards.move: Check every offer term: does it pay you for what the owner actually wants?
cards.trap: Paying a future screener per screen, then getting many weak screens.
cards.memo: **"Show me the incentive, I'll show you the outcome."**
q: How does your guarantee align incentives?
You win when caregivers stay, which is what the owner wants.
clip: Charlie Munger : The power of incentives
cards.clipNote: An interview or clip of the teacher, not from their own channel.

cards.hook: Know exactly **where your competence ends**. Play only games you can win.
cards.plain: A competence without a known edge isn't a competence. Decline whole categories; move what you can't figure out to the too-hard pile.
cards.analogy: Playing your game, not the opponent's.
cards.ex: Buying agencies is in the 2030 plan, not this year's circle.
cards.move: Keep a "too-hard pile" note. New ideas go there until 100 owner conversations.
cards.trap: Mistaking interest in something for competence in it.
q: What do you do with ideas outside your circle?
Put them on the too-hard pile.
clip: Warren Buffett & Charlie Munger: Circle of Competence
cards.clipNote: An interview or clip of the teacher, not from their own channel.

cards.hook: Envy, resentment and self-pity are **self-inflicted poisons**. Avoiding them is an edge.

items: the sin with no fun in it
vis.note: When one shows up: name it, drop it, do the next task.

cards.plain: They blind thinking and kill cheerfulness. Munger deliberately suppressed them as a practical advantage.
cards.analogy: Sulking after a bad call by the umpire costs you the next three games.
cards.ex: Comparing yourself to other 17-year-olds' "easy" lives, or to Hormozi, is envy in disguise.
cards.move: When you catch self-pity ("nobody answers"), say "That's self-pity. Next dial."
cards.trap: Calling self-pity "being honest about how hard it is".
q: Name Munger's three poisons.
Envy, resentment, self-pity (plus anger).
clip: AVOID ENVY, IT HAS NO UPSIDE | RECIPE AGAINST ENVY & JEALOUSY | CHARLIE MUNGER | Ch 5
cards.clipNote: An interview or clip of the teacher, not from their own channel.

cards.hook: The surest way to get what you want is to **deserve it**. The high road is less crowded.
cards.plain: Deserved trust, kept commitments and win-win dealing compound into reputation; tricking people doesn't.
cards.analogy: The coach parents trust gets the referrals.
cards.ex: Never overpromise bench size or checks you didn't do. One lie ends the compounding.
cards.move: Make only promises you can keep this month: replacement in 24h, honest numbers.
cards.trap: Shortcuts that work once.
q: What's the surest way to get what you want?
Deserve it.
clip: Charlie Munger: "To get what you want, you have to DESERVE what you want"
cards.clipNote: An interview or clip of the teacher, not from their own channel.

cards.t: Seek wealth, not money or status
cards.hook: Wealth = **assets that earn while you sleep**. You won't get rich renting out your time.
cards.plain: Money is society's IOU, status is zero-sum. Own equity in a product, business or IP; treat wealth as freedom, not luxury.
cards.analogy: Coaching pays for today. Owning the club pays forever.
cards.ex: Tennis lessons fund the runway; Caregiver Bench (and later agencies) is the equity.
cards.move: Protect the business hours; they're the only hours that build an asset.
cards.trap: Chasing status (looking busy, cool app) instead of ownership.
q: What is wealth according to Naval?
Assets that earn while you sleep.
clip: Seek Wealth, Not Money or Status

cards.hook: Fortunes need leverage: **labor, capital, code, media**. Code and media need no permission.

vis.note: Leverage multiplies judgment: good or bad.

cards.plain: Labor and capital need others' permission and trust; code and media are permissionless and scale to millions.
cards.analogy: One coach, one court vs a training video watched by 10,000 kids.
cards.ex: Your roll-up plan uses labor and capital; War Room is code; documenting your journey is media.
cards.move: For now: one leverage at a time. The phone and your own labor until it works.
cards.trap: Seeking leverage on something that doesn't work yet.
q: Which forms of leverage need no permission?
Code and media.
clip: Pick a Business Model With Leverage

cards.hook: Know-how that **feels like play to you and work to others**. Found by doing, not by courses.
cards.plain: It's learned by apprenticeship and obsession at the edge of a field, not taught in school.
cards.analogy: Your feel for kids' tennis comes from hours on court, not a certificate.
cards.ex: Yours is forming: Florida home care + recruiting + cold calling + building tools.
cards.move: Notice what you do that others find tedious and you don't. Write it down.
cards.trap: Thinking a course gives you specific knowledge. Only doing does.
q: How is specific knowledge found?
By doing and obsession, not by courses.

cards.hook: All returns come from **compounding**: money, relationships, knowledge. That needs repeated games and trust.
cards.plain: Being ethical is long-term greedy: fair dealers become hubs, short-term players get filtered out.
cards.analogy: The club partner you've trained with for years is worth more than ten new ones.
cards.ex: Agency owners you treat well become referrals and, one day, maybe sellers to your roll-up.
cards.move: Treat every owner conversation as the first of many, including the no's.
cards.trap: Squeezing a short-term win from someone you'll meet again.
q: Why is being ethical "long-term greedy"?
Fair dealers become trusted hubs; compounding needs trust.
clip: Play Long-term Games With Long-term People

cards.hook: Leverage multiplies judgment. Being right **85% instead of 70%** wins nearly everything.
cards.plain: Judgment = knowing long-term consequences, built from experience plus honest reflection. Calm minds judge best.
cards.analogy: Shot selection: same strokes, better choices, different results.
cards.ex: Choosing Tampa Bay first, one offer, one channel: judgment calls that save months.
cards.move: After each big decision write the expected result; check it a month later.
cards.trap: More effort on a bad decision.
q: What does leverage multiply?
Judgment, good or bad.

cards.hook: The #1 sleep rule: **same bedtime and wake time every day**, weekends too.
cards.plain: Your body clock likes a fixed rhythm. Regularity matters more than tricks; weekend catch-up shifts the clock and makes Monday worse.
cards.analogy: Same warm-up before every match: the body knows what's coming.
cards.ex: Your plan: 21:00 to 05:20, every day.
cards.move: Tonight and every night: lights out at 21:00, even on Saturday.
cards.trap: "Catching up" on weekends.
q: What's Walker's first sleep rule?
Regularity: same bed and wake time every day.
clip: Sleep Is Your Superpower | Matt Walker | TED

cards.hook: Caffeine lingers for hours. **Last caffeine before 12:00** or it steals deep sleep you don't notice losing.

vis.title: Caffeine still in you at bedtime (rough idea)

cards.plain: You may fall asleep fine yet sleep shallower. Cutting caffeine after noon protects deep sleep.
cards.analogy: Like playing with a slightly loose string: you don't notice, but every shot is a bit worse.
cards.ex: Energy drink before the evening dial block = worse sleep and a worse morning.
cards.move: Any caffeine today: before 12:00.
cards.trap: "Caffeine doesn't affect me."
q: When is your caffeine cutoff?
clip: #1 Sleep Expert: "Even A Little Caffeine Does This To Your Brain & Body!" | Matthew Walker
cards.clipNote: An interview or clip of the teacher, not from their own channel.

cards.t: After a bad night, change nothing
cards.hook: Slept badly? **Same wake time, no nap, same bedtime.** Don't compensate.
cards.plain: Sleeping in or napping pushes the clock and makes the next night worse. Keep the rhythm and the body corrects itself.
cards.analogy: After a bad loss you still show up to the next practice at the usual time.
cards.ex: Your Sleep event: "After a late night: still up at 05:20, no nap, bed 21:00."
cards.move: Next bad night: get up at 05:20 anyway.
cards.trap: Alcohol or a long nap to "fix" it.
q: What do you change after a bad night?
Nothing: same wake time, no nap, same bedtime.
clip: Sleep Is Your Superpower | Matt Walker | TED

cards.t: Prime before the world sets your mood
cards.hook: A short morning ritual: **breathe, feel grateful, see the day's 3 outcomes done.**
cards.plain: Robbins' priming conditions a strong state before email, school and messages decide your mood.
cards.analogy: Warm-up before the match, not after the first lost game.
cards.ex: At 05:30 training: 2 minutes, then the session.
cards.move: Tomorrow 05:30: 3 breaths, 3 gratitudes, 3 outcomes (one is the dial block).
cards.trap: Turning it into a 30-minute ritual you skip.
q: What are the parts of priming?
Breathing, gratitude, seeing the day's outcomes done.
clip: Do This 10-Minute Priming Exercise to Reset Your Entire Life

cards.t: Pick the adaptation, then the variables
cards.hook: Decide **what you're training for** first. Sets, reps and rest follow from that.
cards.plain: Different goals need different settings. Progressive overload drives change; for power, stay fresh and rest fully between sets.
cards.analogy: You don't practise serves the same way for accuracy and for speed.
cards.ex: Wednesday speed day: few reps, full rest, max intent.
cards.move: Write the goal of each training day at the top of the session.
cards.trap: Random hard workouts that build nothing in particular.
q: What drives adaptation over weeks?
Progressive overload.
clip: Essentials: How to Assess & Improve All Aspects of Your Fitness | Dr. Andy Galpin

cards.t: Power work: fresh and fully rested
cards.hook: Power is trained **fresh, fast, with full rest**. Tired reps train slowness.
cards.plain: Sprints, jumps and throws need quality, not fatigue. Low reps, long rest, max speed.
cards.analogy: Serving practice after a 2-hour match teaches a tired serve.
cards.ex: Sprints 6 × 10–20 m with full rest (your Wednesday plan).
cards.move: Next speed session: rest until you feel fully ready before each sprint.
cards.trap: Turning power work into conditioning.
q: How should power sets be rested?
Fully, so every rep is fast.
clip: The Differences in Training for Hypertrophy (Muscle Size) vs. Strength & Power  | Dr. Andy

cards.hook: Galpin calls creatine **foundational**: the best-researched supplement for strength and power.
cards.plain: Daily creatine supports strength and power training. Supplements come after sleep, food and training. Ask a doctor or pharmacist if unsure; this isn't medical advice.
cards.analogy: Good strings: they don't play for you, but they help every shot.
cards.ex: Only after sleep and protein are handled.
cards.move: Check with a parent/doctor before starting anything new.
cards.trap: Supplements to replace sleep and food.
q: What comes before any supplement?
Sleep, food and training.
clip: How & Why to Take Creatine for Brain Injury & Recovery | Dr. Andy Galpin

cards.hook: Train **Zone 2, VO2 max, strength and stability**. Backcast from who you want to be at 80.
cards.plain: Attia plans fitness backwards from the abilities he wants in old age, then builds all four pillars now.
cards.analogy: A complete player: rally stamina, explosive points, power and balance.
cards.ex: Your week already covers strength and speed; easy aerobic work is the gap to check.
cards.move: Look at your week: which pillar has zero sessions?
cards.trap: Only training what you enjoy.
q: Name the four pillars.
Zone 2, VO2 max, strength, stability.

cards.hook: Gain about **0.2–0.4 kg a week** with a small surplus and high protein. Judge by the 7-day average.

vis.note: Our numbers for Egor from Library II, not a prescription.

cards.plain: A moderate surplus with slow gain keeps fat low. Daily weight jumps around; the weekly average tells the truth.
cards.analogy: Building rally consistency: small daily gains, not one heroic session.
cards.ex: ~77 kg → 85 kg is roughly 20–40 weeks at that pace.
cards.move: Weigh each morning, look only at the weekly average on Sunday.
cards.trap: "Dirty bulk": eating everything and gaining fat fast.
q: How do you judge a bulk?
By the 7-day average weight trend.
clip: Can You Gain Muscle in a Calorie Deficit? | Educational Video | Biolayne

cards.hook: Train speed **in tennis patterns**: short bursts, change of direction, recovery steps.
cards.plain: Tennis is short explosive bursts with direction changes. Training should copy those patterns.
cards.analogy: Practising long-distance running for tennis is like practising chess for poker.
cards.ex: Side bounds and short sprints with turns on your speed day.
cards.move: Add one change-of-direction drill to the next speed session.
cards.trap: Long slow jogging as "tennis fitness".
q: What does tennis speed mostly need?
Short bursts with direction changes.
clip: Tennis footwork | Dr. Mark Kovacs taking about the importance of movement and testing

cards.hook: Power needs **both**: strength to push and speed to apply it fast.
cards.plain: Strong but slow, or fast but weak, both cap your power. Periodise blocks through the year.
cards.analogy: A heavy racket swung slowly hits soft.
cards.ex: Monday strength day + Wednesday speed day = power.
cards.move: Keep both days. Don't skip one for the other.
cards.trap: Only lifting heavy, or only doing speed drills.
q: What two qualities make power?
Strength and speed.
clip: Move Quicker, Hit Harder, Recover Faster —  LIVE Q&A with Dr. Mark Kovacs

cards.hook: The serve accelerates the arm; the back of the shoulder must **brake** it. Train the brakes ~3×/week.
cards.plain: Kovacs recommends regular external-rotation and rear-shoulder work to protect serving shoulders.
cards.analogy: A fast car without brakes.
cards.ex: Light band external rotations, 2–3 sets, a few times a week.
cards.move: Add a 5-minute band shoulder routine to 3 sessions this week.
cards.trap: Waiting for pain to start.
q: Why train shoulder decelerators?
To brake the arm after serves and prevent injury.
clip: Mark Kovacs Rotational Athlete Simple Assessment Presented at the 2016 Baseball Conference
cards.clipNote: An interview or clip of the teacher, not from their own channel.

cards.hook: Win with your head: **scout the opponent, have plan A and B, force errors, control tempo.**

steps: speed up or slow down the match

cards.plain: Gilbert's approach: you don't need to outhit everyone. Make them play your game and their weak shots.
cards.analogy: The same as discovery on a sales call: learn before you attack.
cards.ex: Opponent's backhand breaks down on high balls → heavy topspin there.
cards.move: Before your next match or practice set, write plan A and plan B in one line each.
cards.trap: Playing the same way when it's clearly not working.
q: What do you need before a match according to Gilbert?
A scouting report and a plan A and plan B.
clip: Brad Gilbert on Agassi, Coco Gauff, and Winning Ugly

cards.hook: Self 1 (the critic) **interferes**; Self 2 (the body) knows how. Notice, don't judge.
cards.plain: Non-judgmental awareness lets the body correct itself. Give the mind a simple thing to notice instead of instructions.
cards.analogy: Cold calls too: the critic voice before the dial is Self 1.
cards.ex: "Say bounce when it bounces, hit when you hit."
cards.move: In your next lesson, coach a kid with a notice task ("where did the ball land?") instead of a correction.
cards.trap: Judging every shot.
q: What does Self 1 do?
Judges and interferes with the body's learning.
clip: Inner Golf with Tim Gallwey, how to quiet Self 1 before your next round!
cards.clipNote: An interview or clip of the teacher, not from their own channel.

cards.hook: Closing the book and **pulling it out of your head** builds memory. Rereading only feels like learning.

vis.title: What sticks a week later (pattern from research)

cards.plain: Retrieval strengthens the memory you retrieve. That's why every Bootcamp lesson ends closed-book.
cards.analogy: Hitting serves vs watching serve videos.
cards.ex: BAC history: close the notes, write the 5 causes from memory, then check.
cards.move: Next BAC session: 10 minutes reading, 15 minutes recalling and checking.
cards.trap: Rereading because it feels easy.
q: Why does recall beat rereading?
Retrieving strengthens memory; rereading only feels familiar.
clip: Learning how to learn | Barbara Oakley | TEDxOaklandUniversity

cards.hook: The brain learns in **two modes**: focused attention and relaxed wandering. Hard problems need both.
cards.plain: Work hard, then step away. Insights often arrive during the diffuse break, not the 3rd hour of staring.
cards.analogy: The fix for your forehand appears on the drive home.
cards.ex: Stuck on a maths problem: 25 minutes, then a walk.
cards.move: Use the sunlight walk after breakfast as diffuse time for whatever you studied.
cards.trap: Forcing 3 hours straight.
q: When do insights often come?
In diffuse mode, during breaks.
clip: Study Skills - Focused and Diffused Mode (Dr Barbara Oakley)
cards.clipNote: An interview or clip of the teacher, not from their own channel.

cards.hook: Build small **chunks** you can recall in one go, then **mix** problem types instead of blocks.
cards.plain: Chunks are compressed understanding. Interleaving forces you to choose the method, which is what exams demand.
cards.analogy: Mixed drills (forehand, backhand, volley randomly) beat 100 forehands in a row for matches.
cards.ex: Bootcamp's mixed drill is interleaving.
cards.move: Next BAC maths session: mix 3 problem types instead of doing one type 10 times.
cards.trap: Smooth blocked practice that feels like progress.
q: Why does interleaving work?
It trains choosing the method, which exams require.
clip: Learning how to learn | Barbara Oakley | TEDxOaklandUniversity

cards.hook: Learn by **connecting and comparing** from the start, not by memorising facts first.

vis.title: Depth of learning
rungs: use it in a new case

cards.plain: Sung argues for higher-order learning early (relate, compare, evaluate) plus retrieval. Set up the enablers first: sleep, focus, environment.
cards.analogy: Learning a stroke by understanding the swing path, not memorising positions.
cards.ex: History: "how is cause A like cause B?" beats rereading the list.
cards.move: For each BAC topic, write one connection to something you already know.
cards.trap: Memorising disconnected facts.
q: What does Sung put early in learning?
Higher-order thinking: connecting, comparing, evaluating.
clip: How to Remember High Volumes of Information Quickly - 12 Principles

cards.hook: Hard thinking needs **long, distraction-free blocks**. Plan every minute; end with a shutdown.
cards.plain: Newport: do fewer things, block time, protect attention, and close the day with a shutdown ritual.
cards.analogy: A focused 60-minute practice beats 3 hours of chatting on court.
cards.ex: Your 06:15 BAC block and 20:45 shutdown.
cards.move: Next BAC block: phone in another room for the whole block.
cards.trap: "Studying" with notifications on.
q: What ends Newport's workday?
A shutdown ritual.

cards.t: Every action is a vote for who you are
cards.hook: Habits stick when they build an **identity**. Each rep is a vote: "I'm someone who dials."
cards.plain: Don't aim at outcomes first; decide who you are and prove it with small wins.
cards.analogy: You became a tennis player one practice at a time.
cards.ex: 10 dials on a bad day is a vote, even with zero answers.
cards.move: Say tonight: "I'm someone who dials every day." Then cast the vote.
cards.trap: Waiting for a big win to change your identity.
q: What does each action vote for?
The identity you're building.
clip: James Clear - "Every action you take is a vote for the type of person you wish to become."
cards.clipNote: An interview or clip of the teacher, not from their own channel.

cards.hook: Make it **obvious, attractive, easy, satisfying**. Invert them to break a habit.

vis.note: To break a habit: invisible, unattractive, hard, unsatisfying.

cards.plain: Each law removes friction from a good habit; the inverse adds friction to a bad one.
cards.analogy: Racket bag by the door (obvious), music in the car (attractive), shoes on (easy), session ticked (satisfying).
cards.ex: Dial block: War Room opens on Dial (obvious), first number pre-loaded (easy), counter ticks (satisfying).
cards.move: Pick your weakest habit and apply one law tonight.
cards.trap: Relying on motivation instead of design.
q: Name the 4 laws.
Obvious, attractive, easy, satisfying.
clip: James Clear explains The Four Laws of Behavior Change ⚛️ Atomic Habits
cards.clipNote: An interview or clip of the teacher, not from their own channel.

cards.hook: Missing once is an accident. **Missing twice is the start of a new habit.**
cards.plain: Perfection isn't the goal; quick recovery is. The minimum version saves the streak.
cards.analogy: Lost a set? Win the next game.
cards.ex: Missed Tuesday's 100? Wednesday's 10 happen no matter what.
cards.move: If you miss any habit today, write tomorrow's minimum version now.
cards.trap: "I already broke it, so this week is gone."
q: What's Clear's rule after a miss?
Never miss twice.
clip: Atomic Habits: How to Get 1% Better Every Day - James Clear
cards.clipNote: An interview or clip of the teacher, not from their own channel.

cards.hook: Long-term consistency beats short-term intensity. **Start smaller than feels useful.**
cards.plain: Boring routines compound; novelty resets progress. Survive bad days with a minimum version.
cards.analogy: 10 minutes of serves every day beats a 3-hour session once a month.
cards.ex: Minimum day: 10 dials + 25 min BAC.
cards.move: Shrink one habit you keep skipping to a version so small you can't say no.
cards.trap: Restarting with a heroic plan every Monday.
q: What beats short-term intensity?
Long-term boring consistency.
clip: Give me 17 minutes, and I’ll Make You Dangerously Consistent

cards.hook: People say yes because of **reciprocity, consistency, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity, unity.**
cards.plain: These shortcuts are how people decide quickly. Use them honestly: real proof, real limits, real value.
cards.analogy: Parents sign up when other parents (social proof) say the coach (authority) is great.
cards.ex: Free Bench Bulletin (reciprocity), "2 members per area" (scarcity).
cards.move: Find which of the 7 your pitch uses least, and add one honest version.
cards.trap: Fake scarcity or fake proof. One lie kills trust.
cards.memo: **"Give, commit, proof, authority, like, scarce, us."**
q: Which principle is "give first"?
Reciprocity.
clip: Robert Cialdini Explains the Seven Principles of Influence | Brainfluence Brief
cards.clipNote: An interview or clip of the teacher, not from their own channel.

cards.hook: What you put in someone's mind **just before** the ask shapes the answer.
cards.plain: Cialdini: the moment before a message matters as much as the message. Direct attention to what makes the ask feel right.
cards.analogy: Asking a parent to sign up right after their kid's best rally.
cards.ex: Ask "what does an unfilled case cost you?" before mentioning price.
cards.move: On calls: cost-of-problem question first, price second.
cards.trap: Pricing before the problem feels real.
q: What is pre-suasion?
Shaping attention right before the ask.
clip: Robert Cialdini on What is Pre-suasion and Why You Should Use It
cards.clipNote: An interview or clip of the teacher, not from their own channel.

cards.hook: Know what **normal** looks like. Something unusual against that baseline is a signal to act.
cards.plain: Six domains: kinesics (body), biometrics (stress signs), proxemics (distance), geographics (familiarity), iconography (symbols), atmospherics (the room's mood). Judge clusters, not single signs.
cards.analogy: Reading an opponent: a normal toss vs the slight change before a kick serve.
cards.ex: On a call: an owner who's been chatty suddenly goes short = something changed. Ask.
cards.move: In your next tennis group, notice one kid's baseline and one anomaly.
cards.trap: Reading too much into one signal.
q: Why judge clusters?
One signal can mislead; several together are reliable.
clip: EP63 ‘Left of Bang and Situational Awareness’ with Patrick Van Horne
cards.clipNote: An interview or clip of the teacher, not from their own channel.

cards.hook: Every behaviour tries to meet: **certainty, variety, significance, connection, growth, contribution.**

vis.note: Anything that meets 3+ needs becomes addictive.

cards.plain: Your top two needs shape your direction. Understanding someone's needs explains their choices.
cards.analogy: A kid who acts out may need significance, not punishment.
cards.ex: Building app versions meets variety + growth + certainty; dialing feels uncertain. That's why it pulls you.
cards.move: Name your top two needs. Then find how dialing can meet them.
cards.trap: Judging people instead of reading their needs.
q: Why does building War Room pull you more than dialing?
It meets several needs at once (variety, growth, certainty) with no rejection.
clip: These 6 Psychological Needs Control EVERYTHING You Do...

cards.hook: Push back at the **first** jab with the smallest change. Waiting builds resentment until you blow up.

vis.title: Size of the conflict
rows: Say it at the first jab

cards.plain: Like a dog growling before it bites: a calm early signal prevents a big fight later.
cards.analogy: Fixing a grip habit in week one vs after a year.
cards.ex: A kid in your group always late: mention it calmly the second time, not the tenth.
cards.move: Is there one small thing bugging you about someone? Say it calmly this week.
cards.trap: "It's not a big deal" until it is.
q: Why address problems early?
Small calm corrections prevent resentment and blow-ups.

cards.t: Cheap dopamine is the modern devil
cards.hook: Self-help boils down to **choosing long term over short term**. Feeds and games are built to make you lose that choice.
cards.plain: Build boundaries and make the long-term choice pleasant, because willpower alone loses to products designed for attention.
